news.title: Trump makes over 30 deals with NVIDIA shares worth millions of dollars in 9M 2026 — TV
news.text:
NEW YORK, November 24. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump’s accounts have continued to trade NVIDIA in recent months, including "more than three dozen trades buying and selling millions of dollars of NVIDIA stock" in the first nine months of this year, ABC News reported.

The American leader owned shares in the company worth at least $12 mln at the end of 2025, according to his annual financial disclosure report. The White House continues to maintain that third-party institutions manage Trump’s accounts, the TV channel noted.

On November 23, NVIDIA announced that Jensen Huang had been reappointed as president and CEO of the company. On November 12, he stepped down as CEO and president of NVIDIA and resigned from the company’s board of directors amid a scandal over his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China. The Chinese Foreign Ministry dismissed allegations that she worked for Chinese intelligence as slander. According to the Semafor portal, Trump participated in the meeting of the board of directors of NVIDIA before Huang was reinstated as its CEO.
news.summary: The American leader owned shares in the company worth at least $12 mln at the end of 2025, according to his annual financial disclosure report
news.author: Tass

news.title: Iran rejects talks until its seven conditions are fulfilled - parliament speaker
news.text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 24. No steps will be
taken and no negotiations will be held until Iran's seven
conditions for restoring stability and reducing tensions in the
region are fulfilled.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf made the
remarks during a parliamentary session on Tuesday, November 24,
according to the Iranian parliament's information portal.

"Iran is prepared to respond decisively to any action by the
opposing side and, should it make a misstep, to change the
geography of the war," he said.

Ghalibaf said Iran's position was clear and unchanging. He added
that threats against Iranian citizens and increased economic
pressure demonstrated the opposing side's desperation.

The parliamentary speaker also stressed the importance of
preserving national unity and resolving unjustified disagreements
amid the ongoing war.

The remarks come amid renewed tensions between the United States
and Iran, which escalated on July 8.

On that day, the U.S. Armed Forces launched several waves of
strikes on Iranian territory, claiming they were in response to an
attack on a commercial vessel in the Strait of Hormuz. The strikes
marked the first such U.S. military action since a memorandum was
signed between Washington and Tehran.

U.S. President Donald Trump announced the termination of the
ceasefire with Iran on the same day.

In response, Tehran began striking U.S. facilities in Bahrain,
Jordan, Qatar, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Oman.

The conflict has brought maritime trade through the Strait of
Hormuz to a virtual standstill.
news.author: Elnur Baghishov

news.title: Why your energy bills are about to go through the roof
news.text: The cost of living squeeze dominates Brits’ biggest concerns - with soaring energy bills a major worry. Many households are already fearful of turning up the heating now temperatures have plunged, and a worrying number either ration their use - or even don’t put it on at all. Yet any pain being endured now is nothing compared to the frankly frightening jump on the way. Regulator Ofgem will confirm at 7am on Wednesday just how much its price cap will rise by from January 1 - but it’s likely to up something like an average 26%%, or £443 a year, to £2,166 a year. So, what is the price cap and why are energy prices rising so much? Let’s start by staying what it’s not. Ofgem quotes average annual bills but in fact it’s a cap on the unit rate those who it applies to will pay. The unit rate is what you’ll pay for for every kilowatt-hour (kWh) of electricity and gas you use. There’s also a daily standing charge that’s added, and both those make up the tariff. Industry experts Cornwall Insight estimates the unit rate for electricity will rise from 26.32p per kWh to 32.54p , and the daily standing charge will go from 54.83p to 56p. For gas, it forecasts the unit rate will rise from 7.97p per kWh to 10.90p, and the standing charge from 29.68p a day to 31p. When Ofgem last upped its cap in October, it applied to around 34 million energy accounts. Another thing to remember is that the annual figures quoted are slightly meaningless because Ofgem’s cap is reviewed four times a year. So the, say, £2,166 for next year will end being less, or indeed more. What it does impact is prices for January to March, the coldest three months of the year. Industry body Energy UK estimates it will add more than £80 a month, so a potential £240 over the three months. Typical annual dual-fuel bills will be around 120% higher than the average before the 2022 energy crisis caused by Russia ’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine . There have been different reasons in the past, but this time round it’s all about the Middle East war. Wholesale energy prices - gas and electricity - have surged since US President Donald Trump and Israel began the war with the Iran at the end of February. Energy UK says the rise in January is entirely driven by these higher wholesale costs, accounting for almost £1,240 of the average annual bill next year. Although the UK still has its own North Sea gas, the price is impacted by European and international prices, so events well beyond our control. Previous bill increases have also included things like government levies, but Labour has sought to take some of the pressure off households by removing some of those. Of the average expected £2,166 annual bill, nearly £100 will be policy costs, £417 network charges to maintain and upgrade pipes and wires, and £284 operating costs, including covering the bad debts of those household who either don’t - or can’t - pay what they owe. The government has also temporarily removed VAT from the electricity part of bills, a move extended to July, but it’s likely to save the average household just £25 over the winter. Chancellor John Healey, aware of the looming bill shock, used his maiden autumn Budget at the end of October to announce help with energy bills through £100 payments for 20 million households on council bands A to D. It will be paid from January. However, that £100 doesn’t cover the estimated £240 winter bill hike. While welcome, critics say it will help some households who don’t really need extra money and miss more than one miliion vulnerable households who do. Depending on what sort of winter we have, there could be growing calls for more targeted help. Energy UK is arguing for the £150 Warm Home Discount payment to be doubled, at a cost of £900million to the Treasury. Longer term, there are many who think there should be social tariffs or rebates for those most in need. Rising bills will doubtless mean the amount households owe suppliers will jump, too. Along with those who can’t afford to pay their bill is a large amount of debt from households who suppliers can’t track down, because they’re moved on without paying. The average arrears per household increased now stands at £3,485, against around £1,500 before then last energy crisis began. From October to December, all households were paying an average of £67 for suppliers to recover and manage debt. Energy UK reckons total energy debt is likely to rise towards £7billion by the end of 2026, and could hit £8bn next year.
news.summary: Millions of households are about to be hit with an average £240 winter bill shock - but what's driving a massive surge in prices
news.author: Graham Hiscott

news.title: UN food agency warns wars threaten food aid for over seven million people
news.text:
World Food Programme Executive Director Luke Lindberg has warned that shipping chokepoints linked to wars in the Middle East and Ukraine could raise the agency’s costs by $727 million by mid-2027, threatening food aid for 7.3 million more people.

Lindberg, whom US President Donald Trump nominated and the United Nations appointed in September to head the world’s largest humanitarian agency, called for new efforts to safeguard humanitarian shipments of Ukrainian and Russian grain through the Black Sea, modeled on a UN-brokered initiative that was in effect from 2022 to 2023.

Lindberg told the UN Security Council that constraints on food exports and farming inputs passing through the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Black Sea were compounded by climate shocks like El Nino.

“It’s an unthinkable scenario, and it could not come at a worse time,” said Lindberg, a former US agriculture official, urging diplomats to focus on trying to find rapid solutions to ensure some 10 million tons of Ukrainian and Russian grain that were already in silos reached people in need.

He said 266 million people globally were already suffering from acute hunger and there was a risk of famine in parts of Sudan, South Sudan, and Somalia.

Lindberg told Reuters in an interview that it was critical to resolve the situation in the Black Sea, one of the world’s breadbasket regions whose grains were vital to countries like Somalia and Yemen, which imports 90% of its food.

He urged diplomats to work on a humanitarian corridor similar to the Black Sea Grain Initiative, a UN-brokered deal agreed in ​July 2022 ​that allowed ⁠the safe export of nearly 33 million metric tons of ​Ukrainian grain. Russia withdrew from the agreement in 2023, complaining that its own ⁠food ​and fertilizer exports faced ​serious obstacles.

‘Untenable’

Lindberg told Reuters that any revived agreement would have to cover both Russian and Ukrainian exports to win acceptance.

“It’s untenable to have full grain silos in Ukraine and Poland and the region, and then you have empty stomachs in other parts of the world ... If a diplomatic solution can be reached, we stand ready to move grain from both Russia and Ukraine,” he said.

The WFP head added Black Sea food shipments were down sharply this year, with 63% fewer wheat and maize vessels moving through the Bosphorus as of mid-October than at the same point in 2025. Over 300 attacks had been recorded and at least 40 crew members had been killed, he said.

That meant some 10 million tons of Russian and Ukrainian wheat might not reach global markets this year — enough to feed 44 million people, he said.

Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics said his country, which holds the current rotating presidency of the Security Council, would back a new Black Sea initiative to get grain out of Ukraine and increase maritime security, underscoring the “very dire situation” facing developing countries in Africa and Asia.

“If that is possible, we would be applauding such or any of initiatives. Whether that’s going to happen or not remains to be seen. But some efforts are ongoing. Unfortunately, I don’t see momentum as we speak today,” he told Reuters in an interview.

The food price index of the UN‘s Food and Agriculture Organization had hit a near four-year high this September, wheat prices were up almost 10% from January, and higher energy and transport costs had increased grocery prices, especially in import-dependent and food-insecure countries, Lindberg said.

Food yields will likely also be lower next season, given constraints in global fertilizer supplies, of which 30% flow through the Strait of Hormuz, he added.

The wars were taking a direct toll on WFP’s humanitarian operations and sharply increasing its costs, he said. The WFP has already lowered its target to provide food assistance to 91 million people in 2027 from 110 million people this year, but higher costs could drive that number even lower, he said.

The agency’s total costs last year were nearly $12.2 billion, so $727 million in additional costs by mid-2027 would mark an increase of nearly 6%. That number could rise further unless current conditions changed, the agency said.
news.summary: Global wars are raising transport costs and keeping grain from markets
news.author: Andrea Shalal,Moiz Salhi

news.title: Twenty-one states sue Trump administration over housing rule that could evict U.S. citizen children
news.text:
Twenty-one states and Pennsylvania's governor have sued the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development over a rule that would deny federal housing assistance to families if any household member lacks eligible citizenship or immigration status.

The states say the rule could split up families or evict U.S. citizens from public housing. States including California, New York, Arizona and Massachusetts joined the suit.

HUD defends the rule, arguing illegal immigrants are taking advantage of the current eligibility requirements. The rule takes effect on Dec. 14. It would require people to verify their citizenship or eligible immigration status to receive federal housing assistance.

“No child should lose their home over a parent's immigration status,” said California Attorney General Rob Bonta during a press conference. “This rule is cruel, and it’s unlawful." 

For over three decades, Congress has authorized prorated federal housing assistance for mixed-status families, whose members have different citizenship or immigration statuses. These families receive less assistance if a household member is ineligible because of their immigration status.

The new rule would ban mixed-status families from receiving any assistance. “Picture a mom with two kids in public housing. All U.S. citizens. Their dad is not eligible. Under this rule, all four of them lose their home,” Bonta said.

One in five children in California is part of a mixed-status family, Bonta said, estimating the rule will affect 7,000 households in his state. The new rule would also require public housing authorities and private landlords to report tenants who fail verification to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

“Congress never gave HUD the power to throw mixed-status families out of their homes or turn private landlords into immigration enforcement. But that’s exactly what this rule does,” Bonta said. The new rule is the latest in a series of moves by President Donald Trump's administration targeting legal immigrants.

Those moves include restricting healthcare, nutrition benefits and other subsidies while stripping legal protections from some immigrant groups to make more people eligible for deportation. HUD Secretary Scott Turner first announced the proposed rule in January, but the department finalized it only last week.

“HUD’s final rule fully implements the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act and ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars. This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing. This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist," said Turner in an emailed statement on Monday.

Earlier this year, HUD conducted an audit with DHS and identified 20,000 mixed-status households receiving federally funded housing assistance nationwide. The department said illegal immigrants were using “loopholes” to access benefits while the department struggled to provide housing for all who need it.
news.summary: Twenty states and the have sued the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development over a new rule requiring citizenship verification for federal housing assistance
news.author: Mikella Schuettler

news.title: Jensen Huang Back At Nvidia After 11 Days. He's Not The First CEO To Return
news.text: Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned as CEO, following revelations of extramarital affairs with one of his direct reports and a suspected Chinese spy.Huang left the company on November 12. On Monday, Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated him, following discussions with Huang and pressure from US President Donald Trump. The 11-day turnaround makes it one of the fastest high-profile CEO comebacks.Still, that kind of boomerang isn't unheard of. Recent corporate history is littered with founder-CEOs who were reinstated after directors and investors decided the business couldn't do without them. Some returned after a successor struggled; others after the board faced external pressure.Photo Credit: BloombergBoards sometimes conclude that a former leader is a safer bet than an outside candidate or planned internal successor. A returning founder can bring institutional knowledge, relationships with employees and investors and a degree of authority that a newly appointed CEO may struggle to replicate. Here are five noteworthy precedents: Sam Altman, OpenAI OpenAI's board abruptly fired Altman in 2023, citing concerns about his candor in communications with the board. The decision prompted an employee revolt: More than 700 employees threatened to leave for Microsoft unless Altman was reinstated. OpenAI announced an agreement in principle for his return less than a week later, along with a new board. The episode demonstrated how employees, investors and commercial partners can exert pressure on a board's decision to remove a founder.Photo Credit: BloombergBob Iger, DisneyIger stepped down as Disney CEO in 2020 after 15 years in the role, handing the position to his handpicked successor, Bob Chapek. In 2022, Disney's board abruptly removed Chapek and brought Iger back, citing the need for leadership during a difficult period of industry transformation. The decision was a striking reversal of a succession plan that Iger himself had orchestrated.Photo Credit: BloombergHoward Schultz, StarbucksSchultz stepped down as CEO in 2000, although he remained chairman. He returned as CEO in 2008 amid declining sales, and stayed until 2017. He returned yet again as interim CEO in 2022, making him a prominent example of a founder repeatedly reclaiming the top job.Photo Credit: BloombergJack Dorsey, TwitterDorsey was pushed out as Twitter CEO in October 2008 amid concerns about his management. He remained chairman. Dorsey returned as CEO in 2015 while also running the payments company Square. His return is an example of a board turning back to a founder who had been sidelined but never entirely left the company's orbit.Photo Credit: BloombergSteve Jobs, AppleJobs was forced out of Apple in 1985 after a power struggle with then-CEO John Sculley. Jobs rejoined Apple in 1996 when it acquired NeXT, a company he founded, and was named interim CEO in 1997 and permanent CEO in 2000. His return is arguably the most famous corporate comeback in American business history.Photo Credit: BloombergDisney's Iger and OpenAI's Altman are particularly relevant because their returns followed boards reversing decisions about their successors. Huang's reinstatement similarly reverses a major leadership decision.Huang's case is distinctive because the US government played a direct role in the board's deliberations."I can't think of a single example where a US president or somebody in the administration came forward and said we want a particular person to take over a company," said Michael Useem, emeritus professor of management at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School. "In this case, it's not a company that is partly owned by the US or in any way is beholden to the US. Strictly speaking, Donald Trump is a complete outsider on this, but nonetheless, he weighed in. So it's a unique one-off event."But, Useem added, "One wonders, is this going to be precedent-setting? Such that as future board decisions are up for consideration [US government officials may] decide to weigh in on companies that are completely privately owned."(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: Huang left the company on November 12. On Monday, Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated him, following discussions with Huang and pressure from US President Donald Trump.

news.title: Court clears Army to blow up tons of toxic bomb chemicals in Iowa as Trump pressures incoming governor
news.text:
A federal appeals court has granted permission for the U.S. Army to detonate tons of degraded explosive materials at an ammunition plant in Iowa.

The order from the 8th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals was one of two rulings President Donald Trump indicated he was awaiting after directing the military on Monday to pause the chemical disposal pending judicial review.

The president noted that his determination remains contingent upon agreement from incoming Gov.-elect Rob Sand, warning that federal authorities would otherwise be forced to proceed with the planned detonation.

Initial plans to destroy 68 barrels of lead azide were set for last Friday, but the Army postponed the operation three times following significant public concern regarding potential health and environmental hazards.

The revised plan aimed for a Wednesday detonation ahead of Thanksgiving to take advantage of favorable weather.

President Donald Trump announced on Monday that his administration would defer to a federal appeals court prior to moving ahead with the disposal of the degraded bomb-making material at the Iowa facility.

The scheduled neutralization of the 68 lead azide drums has been delayed three times after sharp public apprehension over environmental and health risks.

While military personnel sought a Wednesday timeline due to weather conditions, the Army did not immediately comment on the president's statement.

"At the same time, have ordered the military not to do so until such time as the 8th Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Gov.-elect Rob Sand agreeing to the operation," Trump said.

He warned that if consent is withheld, the administration will halt the procedure, holding Sand responsible for "any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation."

Sand responded in a social media post, writing that past administrative choices meant "No good options exist and the situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been."

He raised questions over why a contract intended to eliminate the hazard was canceled and "why we are rushing to demolition now in late November."

The delay follows a legal challenge from environmental groups, who secured a stay from the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals to review an emergency permit granted by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

Trump indicated a preference for quick disposal via a controlled explosion, describing it as the safer option.

However, he confirmed that the operation remains paused pending judicial and state clearance.

Sand stressed, "The safety of Iowans should be the top priority of everyone involved," adding that "All relevant federal, state and local government resources should be focused on protecting everyone that could be impacted."

Near the Middletown facility, some residents have taken preventive steps by sealing windows and doors against potential lead dust, while others expressed worry online about wind carrying potential plumes.

Officials acknowledged the toxicity of lead, advising residents to stay indoors during any explosion and to wash down outdoor surfaces with water.

In court documents, Army Col. Aaron Teller, a munitions emergency specialist, explained that reduced liquid inside the barrels leaves the substance susceptible to freezing, raising the sensitivity of crystals near the lids.

"Even a small amount of friction can break the crystal formation, causing an explosive chain reaction," he stated.

The barrels were initially discovered in March.

Although EPA records show chemical neutralization options were evaluated, officials determined that moving the drums posed a severe risk of an accidental blast. Environmentalists contend that alternative methods were overlooked, while officials warn that the danger of an explosion grows as temperatures fall below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1 Celsius).
news.summary: Initial plans to destroy 68 barrels of lead azide were set for last Friday, but the Army postponed the operation three times following significant public concern regarding potential health hazards
news.author: Susan Montoya Bryan

news.title: Trump Says Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Has ‘Worked It Out’ With His Wife
news.text:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has reportedly reconciled with his wife, Lori, after allegations that he had affairs with at least three women.

Huang, 63, unexpectedly stepped down from his role at the artificial intelligence company on November 12 after acknowledging an affair with Alice Huang, a woman suspected by US officials of spying for China. The two are not related.

Subsequent reports alleged that Huang had also been involved with Nvidia vice president Kimberly Powell and a third, unnamed employee.

Nvidia’s board returned Huang to the CEO position on Monday morning, following President Donald Trump’s public call for the company to reinstate him.

Trump has since said that Huang’s wife, Lori, 64, chose to remain with him despite the allegations of infidelity.

‘He has a very, very, very good wife, and they’ve worked it out,’ Trump told The New York Times. ‘She’s a fantastic woman.’

Trump, who has previously acknowledged infidelity during his first marriage to Ivana Trump while involved with Marla Maples, also suggested Huang had mishandled the situation by resigning.

‘I wouldn’t have handled it the way he handled it,’ Trump said. ‘Without that, it would have been a lot easier because that got the attention. You know, sex was involved, and sex sells better than stocks.’

Jensen and Lori Huang met at Oregon State University, where they were assigned as laboratory partners in an electrical engineering course. Huang was 17 at the time.

By the time Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993, the couple had welcomed their two children, Madison and Spencer.

Madison and Spencer now occupy senior roles in important business divisions at Nvidia. Lori serves as president of the family’s $9 billion charitable foundation and regularly attends public events alongside her husband.

The timing of Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, remains unclear. The pair were first photographed together at a Taipei bar in June 2024.

They were reportedly seen together again in May 2025, leaving a Taipei restaurant after a dinner involving AI suppliers.

Earlier this month, reports said US intelligence agencies suspected Alice Huang of helping move restricted, advanced Nvidia chips into China by circumventing export controls.

Officials reportedly believed she had been positioned to obtain sensitive information from Jensen Huang while influencing Nvidia’s business decisions in ways that could expand China’s access to advanced AI hardware. Beijing has rejected the allegations.

Trump said on Monday that the federal government had ‘no reason to believe’ Huang’s return to Nvidia created a national security threat.

‘The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the US Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct,’ Trump wrote.

‘On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure.’

Trump said he had personally intervened with Nvidia’s board before Huang’s reinstatement, including speaking with board members on Sunday night.

He also said Vice President JD Vance held private discussions with Huang over the weekend at his request.

Trump claimed Vance helped obtain the assurances Nvidia’s directors needed that the US government did not regard Huang as a national security risk.

In his interview with the Times, Trump said Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton already knew about the investigation into Huang before he became involved.

‘All those guys knew about it,’ he said. ‘I had to go to them before I recommended this. Look, I can’t do this and then all of a sudden have somebody get indicted for, for whatever.’

Trump said Blanche and Clayton had been examining the allegations involving Alice Huang for a ‘long time’ and insisted he would not have intervened if officials had found evidence of wrongdoing.

Earlier on Monday, the president described Huang’s return as the ‘correct and proper decision.’ In a social media post, he said the United States ‘needs Jensen’s leadership’ at Nvidia to support the company’s success as well as the wider American economy.

Trump also called on Nvidia to continue its ‘thorough internal investigation’ into compliance with US export restrictions and to ensure the company is safeguarding national security.

The president separately shared the altered image of Huang, which borrowed its imagery from photographs of Trump raising his fist after surviving an assassination attempt. In the parody, Huang was shown clutching a red bra.

Huang returned to Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters on Monday, where employees gathered in the atrium and cheered loudly, according to an employee video aired by CNBC.

‘I am going to be a better CEO the second time around,’ Huang told staff.

In a statement, Huang said he was ‘honored’ to return to Nvidia. He said he was taking up the responsibility with ‘the greatest humility and renewed commitment’ and would also serve as the company’s president.

He thanked board chairman Harvey C. Jones and interim chief executive Colette Kress, who will return to her position as chief financial officer, along with Nvidia’s senior leadership for guiding the company through the brief upheaval.

‘I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support,’ Huang said.

‘Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.’

news.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang pulls off unlikely comeback in just 11 days
news.text: New York: Nvidia's surprise move to bring back Jensen Huang capped an unlikely comeback bid for the celebrity CEO, whose campaign to reclaim the top job following his resignation foundered before the White House intervened.Huang, a company co-founder, stepped down after reports of extramarital affairs including one with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of working as a spy for Beijing.Just 11 days after announcing his resignation and six days after rejecting his offer to return as CEO, Nvidia's board of directors on Monday said Huang had returned as CEO, effective immediately.President Donald Trump claimed credit for Huang's reinstatement to the helm of a company at the centre of the artificial intelligence boom, saying in an interview Monday with CNBC: “The board decided to do what we wanted them to do.”Here's a look at how Huang's comeback unfolded.Huang resigned as pressure mounted on several frontsNvidia announced Huang's resignation on Nov. 12, effective immediately, replacing him in the interim with Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer and an executive vice president. The board of directors also named its first-ever chairman, Harvey C. Jones, an investor and entrepreneur.Earlier that week, Trump said the FBI was investigating but he remained complimentary of Huang, saying he “has done a fantastic job.” Days earlier, Nvidia's board announced its own investigation into the allegations but said it remained confident in Huang's leadership.But pressure compounded late Wednesday after reports surfaced of another alleged affair by Huang, this time involving an Nvidia employee who reported to him.A petition campaign emerged to reinstate HuangA “Stand with Jensen” petition drive that started the day after the resignation announcement picked up steam, gaining signatures from many current and former Nvidia staff, investors and other Silicon Valley supporters, including SpaceX founder Elon Musk.It called on the board to bring back Huang while an independent investigation proceeded or until there was “compelling evidence” that his departure was in the company's best interests. Trump himself weighed in on Nov. 16, saying Huang “learned a big lesson” and he “would certainly not mind” if he was reinstated.In his first public statements since his departure, Huang posted a statement Nov. 17 on social media saying he would be “honoured” to return as CEO if the board decided it was in the company's best interests. He acknowledged making “serious mistakes” in his personal life. Nvidia's board firmly rejected the idea of a comebackLater on the same day, during a quarterly earnings call, Nvidia rejected Huang's offer to return as CEO. Jones, the company chairman, said the board of directors “unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”That same day, key House lawmakers said Huang had voluntarily agreed to appear for transcribed interviews as the company faced intensifying scrutiny over sales of its advanced computer chips and the implications for national security. Publicly and behind the scenes, Trump continued lobbying for HuangOver the weekend, Trump posted on social media that he hoped the board would rehire Huang. “It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the USA,” he wrote.After Huang was reinstated, the president disclosed he had been working behind the scenes as well. Trump said he spoke to Huang about the reinstatement Sunday, and the CEO assured him that he would work harder than before his fall. Trump also said his administration assured Nvidia that there were no national security concerns about Huang's return.In its statement announcing Huang's reinstatement, the company said: “In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

news.title: Jensen Huang’s return has calmed markets but fears of an AI bubble still run deep
news.text:
The next few weeks could determine whether Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO was the prudent one that cheering employees, shareholders and US President Donald Trump made it out to be – or a big mistake.

Huang’s supporters argued that he was indispensable, not only to the company but to the entire AI industry, at the moment a major engine of the economy. 

But he carries some baggage Nvidia still has to deal with.

Huang likely violated the company's code of conduct. He acknowledged having an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. And national security issues aside, Huang’s unusual management style, which included striking deals with a mere handshake, would have doomed many other CEOs.

It’s not a given that Huang's second go-round will survive congressional investigations, lawsuits and a probe by a law firm hired by his own board. But investors pushed Nvidia shares up 31.5 percent on Monday and Nvidia employees chanted Huang’s name as he returned to headquarters.

Here is how Huang came back despite the odds, why he's widely seen as irreplaceable, and the challenges he still faces.

'Serious mistakes'

Soon after Huang resigned on November 12, the campaign for his return began. A petition started making the rounds in Silicon Valley with employees and celebrity leaders, including SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, arguing for a comeback.

“I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote on social media early last week, while acknowledging he had made “serious mistakes”.

The company refused the offer.

Then came help from a US president who measures his success in no small part by investor returns and didn't like what he was seeing.

Nvidia stock was collapsing, down a third since November 9, and suddenly fears mounted that an AI bubble was popping. By Friday, the broader S&P 500 had fallen more than 10 percent from its recent high, the definition of a market correction.

“The board decided to do what we wanted them to do,” Trump said on CNBC on Monday of his lobbying efforts over the weekend. "I believe my intervention was very important.” 

Watch moreWhy the Nvidia scandal is bad news for Europe’s AI ambitions

On Monday, the S&P 500 jumped 4.7 percent, enough to recover over half its loss from last week, which was one of the worst since the 2008 financial crisis. When asked if the falling market influenced his thinking in bringing Huang back, Trump told CNBC, “probably so”.

"You've basically had ‌this perfect storm of uncertainty that has created a crisis of confidence," said King Lip, chief strategist at BakerAvenue Wealth Management in San Francisco.

"This ⁠Nvidia fallout was one of those pieces of ... uncertainty. So this removes a pretty significant one with Jensen coming back."

One reason Silicon Valley luminaries pushed for Huang's return was he was considered an extraordinary deal-maker.

“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Musk wrote on X. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

'Nobody had the big picture perspective'

Huang ran the company like a small business, including having an astounding 60 people report directly to him and employing three family members. And he himself boasted of his personal, idiosyncratic style, saying of TSMC, the giant Taiwanese company making Nvidia chips, “We don't have a contract, and that's pretty great.” 

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the leadership expert at the Yale School of Management, has a different opinion.

“His lack of contracts for hundreds of millions of dollars of business is unparalleled in history – and there's no reason for it,” said Sonnenfeld, adding that the dozens of direct reports was “absurd” too.

“It made sure that nobody had the big picture perspective.”

Another aspect of Huang's tenure also explains why so many wanted to see him return: he became essential to the AI economy by propping up customers and suppliers.

Many AI companies buying Nvidia chips, including the newly public Anthropic, don't make a profit and have been burning through cash quickly in operating their businesses. Enter Nvidia and its vast resources. It helped them buy its chips by striking deals to buy computing capacity and other services from them in turn.

Such arrangements are called circular financing, and they pose big dangers for investors – a fact admitted by Nvidia itself in a recent report in which it warned it may have no use for “all the capacity we are committed to purchase”.

Read moreThe Nvidia affair: Are markets about to fall out of love with AI?

Nvidia has been tied to an array of companies involved in the sprawling AI buildout. It bought shares in data centre operator CoreWeave, South Korean internet and cloud service provider Naver and more besides.

Those stocks rose on news of ​Huang's return, but not enough to recover losses logged since his resignation, suggesting investors are still nervous about the outlook for Nvidia's financing of customers and the broader AI trade.

XTB analyst Kathleen Brooks says Huang is considered key to keeping this financial ecosystem running.

“His return suggests more of the same when it comes to circular financing and the rapid AI infrastructure build out,” wrote Brooks in a report, adding, “The market loves it.”

For its part, Nvidia's board said it “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

“All is right in the world again,” wrote Cantor Fitzgerald financial analyst CJ Muse in a report after Huang's return, “and a very happy day.”

Maybe, but fears of an AI bubble are still rife, and investigations into Huang, his board and Trump administration officials who approved of Nvidia chip sales are looming. 

One focus is Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is in charge of export controls and is a Huang booster and whose former company, Cantor, helps finance Nvidia customers.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat who called Huang's restoration “reckless”, says the banking committee she will head next year will be digging into whether Nvidia has complied with export controls.

She also said the Trump administration “needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement”. 

(FRANCE 24 with AP and Reuters)

news.title: Trump held at least $12 million in Nvidia stock while pressing for Jensen Huang's return - report
news.text:
According to the annual financial report published overnight on Tuesday by ABC News, President Donald Trump held at least $12 million worth of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025.

According to the report, Trump continued trading Nvidia shares in recent months, buying and selling the company’s stock more than 35 times, with investments totaling millions of dollars through September. The White House, however, continues to insist that a third party manages Trump’s accounts.

“President Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions. All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle said.

He further claimed that “Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers.”

Against the backdrop of the betrayal scandals and the Chinese spy affair, Trump repeatedly intervened on behalf of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, culminating Monday in his taking credit for Huang’s return to Nvidia. He said he had spoken “directly and indirectly” with members of the company’s board about Huang’s return to the role.

Following the announcement of Huang’s return to his role, Wall Street’s major stock indexes rebounded sharply after the weekend crash, and Nvidia’s stock surged by no less than 30% yesterday.

The Dow Jones index closed up 1,447.98 points, or 3.0%; the S&P 500 surged 4.73%, and the Nasdaq jumped 6.5%.

news.title: Heating oil update as 6 ‘steps’ to protect households this winter confirmed
news.text: The government has confirmed ‘steps’ it is taking to protect households this winter that use heating oil. The oil is used to heat more than 1.5 million homes in the UK. Prices have more than doubled in the last year, mostly due to Donald Trump's Iran war - and there is no price cap as there is for many gas and electricity customers. Kerosene is the most widely used fuel in domestic central heating systems in the UK. It is typically used in homes not connected to the mains gas grid - often in rural areas. The government has been pressed over what steps are being taken to protect users of heating oil from rising prices this winter. Now it has issued a response explaining six measures that could support households that are eligible. The matter was raised by Lib Dem Harrogate MP Tom Gordon, who asked the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero what steps it is “taking to protect households that use heating oil from price rises this winter.” Polly Billington, a minister in the department, has now set out six steps that the government says it is taking to offer help. They provide a recap of what support it has announced. These are: A £100 payment for eligible households £100 million to councils that can offer support to homes struggling with energy bills £53 million of targeted support for heating oil users The extension of an energy VAT cut Measures that cut £150 from energy bills And plans to regulate the heating oil sector Ms Billington said in a response issued on Wednesday, November 18: “The Government recognises the significant pressures heating oil price increases place on rural households, and given the volatility of global fossil fuel markets, provided breathing space for off-grid households through the measures announced at the Autumn Budget . “The £100 Household Energy Payment will reach eligible households in England living in their main home in Council Tax bands A to D from January 2027. It supports eligible households regardless of heating source as eligibility does not depend on having a gas account. Therefore, households who use heating oil can also receive this support if they meet the criteria. “Furthermore, an additional £100 million enables councils to provide discretionary support to households struggling with energy bills who are ineligible for the core payment. This comes on top of the £53 million of targeted support announced in March for heating oil users, with £27 million made available to local authorities in England via the Crisis and Resilience Fund. “Off-gas-grid households with domestic electricity meters also benefit from the extension of the existing VAT cut on electricity to 1 July 2027, and last year’s Budget measures removing an average of £150 of costs from household energy bills. “The Government also published its formal response to the Competition and Markets Authority’s heating oil report on 13 October and is taking forward proposals to regulate the heating oil sector for the first time, ensuring households are treated fairly.” The government announced in October that there would be stronger protections for heating oil consumers in new codes of conduct for the industry. It also said minimum order volumes as high as 500 litres for some customers would be reviewed. At the time of the announcement, the government also said: “Heating oil customers are also eligible for extra support to get onto homegrown clean energy, after the government increased its discount off the cost of a heat pump to £9,000 for households who use heating oil.” For more on the heat pump scheme, see the gov.uk announcement here . news.title: Huang return keeps China hawks at bay
news.text:
Donald Trump’s intervention that persuaded Nvidia to restore Jensen Huang as chief executive has put Washington’s long-dominant China hawks on the back foot. For now.

China hawks at bay

The news on Monday that Jensen Huang was returning to head Nvidia boosted the price of the company’s shares by 30 per cent, at one stage adding almost $1 trillion to its stock market valuation. 

But beneath the soaring chorus of joy on Wall Street could be heard the sombre countermelody of wailing and rending of garments on Capitol Hill.

Huang’s return came less than two weeks after his abrupt departure following his admission to two extramarital relationships, one with a woman who was alleged to have links with China’s spy agency, the ministry for state security. Trump said on Monday that he had convinced Nvidia to bring Huang back after the fallout from his departure had triggered an extended sell-off of shares in AI companies.

The case against Huang was driven by a succession of news reports citing US intelligence claims that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman based in Singapore with whom he became romantically involved, may have been spying for Beijing. Subsequent reports suggested that the US intelligence agencies were not sure if she was a spy, with some speculating that Beijing’s spies only became interested in her after she got involved with the Nvidia boss.

Trump appeared sceptical from the start, portraying Huang’s fall as a personal tragedy rather than a national security breach and casting doubt on the espionage claims.

“Every time you have a Chinese woman that’s good looking or beautiful, they say she’s a spy,” he said.

“With Jensen, I don’t believe that’s true.”

But days after Huang’s departure from Nvidia, the White House tightened restrictions on the export of advanced microchips to China, banning their use by Chinese companies in third countries such as Singapore and Malaysia. 

Alice Huang’s firm Megaspeed used advanced Nvidia chips in data centres in southeast Asia where Chinese companies could rent computing power to train their AI models and the new controls closed the loophole that made that practice legal.

Huang’s fall appeared to tilt the balance within the Trump administration away from figures like commerce secretary Howard Luttnick who wanted to allow Nvidia to sell more chips to China and towards the more hawkish treasury secretary Scott Bessent and secretary of state Marco Rubio. And the spying allegations emboldened those in Congress who view the contest for supremacy in AI between the US and China exclusively through the lens of national security.

Both parties on Capitol Hill became more hawkish on China during Trump’s first term and the trend continued under Joe Biden, who prioritised efforts to limit Chinese access to advanced technology. Huang last year persuaded Trump to allow Nvidia to sell some more of its chips to China, although the most advanced models remained restricted.

Trump’s intervention on Huang’s behalf on Monday drew criticism from both Democrats and Republicans in Congress, who made clear that they will continue to investigate the Nvidia boss. The new Democratic intake who will take their seats in January include some who favour a less confrontational approach to China but they are unlikely to shift the congressional balance on the issue.

Even if Trump pursues a more moderate policy towards Beijing in the remaining two years of his term as president, a Democratic successor is likely to return to the hawkish approach pursued by Biden. Foreign policy advisers in Washington can survive their most calamitous decisions in office, even if countless innocent people far away do not, and their impressive record of failure will not prevent many in Biden’s team from returning to the White House under the next Democratic president.

news.title: Ukraine Drone Strike on Russian Warship in Libya Risks ‘Serious Escalation,’ Ex-Official Warns
news.text:
A Ukrainian sea-drone attack that capsized and sank a Russian warship in Libya on Sunday could represent a “serious escalation” in the nearly five-year conflict, according to a former U.S. national security adviser. The former official characterized the operation as a “giant tantrum” by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Morgan Murphy, a former press secretary to the secretary of defense, told News Outlet that the overnight strike on the Russian corvette Mercury at the Libyan port of Benghazi could place additional pressure on ties between Zelenskyy and President Donald Trump. Murphy said the incident also reflected tensions that had surfaced during former President Joe Biden’s administration.

“The attack on the Russian corvette Mercury in North Africa — specifically in Libya — marks a serious escalation of the war in Ukraine,” Murphy said.

Murphy said describing the Benghazi operation as a “giant tantrum” was one possible interpretation, adding that such conduct was “not unusual” for Zelenskyy.

Murphy also contended that Zelenskyy’s willingness to pursue military actions that complicate U.S. diplomatic priorities has irritated successive administrations in Washington.

“That is why I believe both the Biden and Trump administrations have been frustrated with Zelenskyy,” Murphy said. “He is operating as an independent actor rather than as an ally.”

Reports said Biden became angry during a June 2022 phone call after Zelenskyy sought more military assistance soon after the White House announced a $1 billion aid package for Ukraine.

In a memoir published recently, Biden likewise described private frustrations with Zelenskyy, portraying the Ukrainian president as moody, stubborn and less appreciative than expected.

Murphy said the Benghazi strike could further complicate Trump’s efforts to negotiate an end to the war, especially after the president held a historic summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping without Zelenskyy.

“The president had a successful meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, and he met with them without Zelenskyy, as is his prerogative as president of the United States,” Murphy said.

“Zelenskyy was clearly unhappy about that, and this attack may have been his way of reminding the president that Ukraine remains highly relevant.”

The operation was reportedly carried out by Ukraine’s SBU intelligence service and armed forces against the Russian vessel while it was in port. The attack has raised questions about the drones’ launch point and whether the conflict could extend even farther beyond Ukraine’s borders.

Zelenskyy praised the operation in a post on X Monday, calling it “an exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war.”

Murphy said Zelenskyy is under growing pressure to show that Kyiv can still achieve major battlefield successes as Trump seeks a diplomatic path toward ending the conflict.

“I believe he is seeking a victory because Ukraine has attracted more international aid and sympathy when it has been winning,” Murphy said.

Ukraine received broad international backing after resisting Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, surprising those who expected Moscow to overrun Kyiv quickly.

“Ukraine performed far better than expected against an enemy five times its size, and people naturally rally around an underdog.”

Murphy said the Russian invasion’s early failures produced “a tremendous wave of sympathy — and, more importantly, support — for Ukraine.”

However, Murphy said Ukraine has found it harder to maintain that early momentum as the war has continued, evolving into what he called a “stalemate and a war of attrition.”

“Zelenskyy is facing greater difficulty building support,” Murphy said.

“After watching the president meet with Russia and Xi Jinping in China, he needed a victory — and he needed a dramatic one. That made an asymmetric attack an attractive option.”

The Benghazi operation also highlights Ukraine’s growing ability to strike Russian military targets thousands of miles away, although the precise method remains unclear.

“Ukraine has claimed responsibility, but officials have been deliberately vague about where the attack originated,” Murphy said.

“Some believe it was launched from inside Libya. Others argue it came from a mothership, which is entirely plausible — perhaps an ordinary-looking cargo vessel used to deploy the drones.”

Murphy said the strike illustrates a larger transformation in modern warfare, as military leaders work to understand the impact of increasingly advanced drone operations.

“We are witnessing a fundamental and unprecedented change in warfare as it happens,” he said.

“It will take time for military planners and nations to determine how best to respond to this type of aggression.”

Beyond the battlefield consequences, Murphy warned that the strike could damage Washington’s diplomatic efforts to negotiate an end to the war.

“A determined group of diplomats and policy thinkers in Washington wants to see a diplomatic resolution to this conflict sooner rather than later,” Murphy said.

“They believe that outcome would serve the interests of the United States and the world, but above all, the interests of the Ukrainian people.”

Murphy said advocates of a negotiated settlement would probably regard the reported Libyan strike as a blow to Trump’s peace initiative.

“Many influential voices in Washington want the war to end, and they will view this escalation in Libya as working against the president’s efforts.”

news.title: Turkmen president, US deputy secretary discuss trade and investment ties
news.text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 24. Turkmen
President Serdar Berdimuhamedov and US Deputy Secretary of State
Christopher Landau have discussed opportunities to expand bilateral
trade and investment cooperation, the press service of the Turkmen
government reported.

According to the report, the meeting took place in Ashgabat
during Landau's visit to Turkmenistan. The sides noted the
development of bilateral relations across political, economic and
cultural areas, highlighting the potential to increase mutual trade
and strengthen investment ties.

Landau said that agreements reached during talks between the
presidents of the two countries last year were already producing
positive results.

The meeting also highlighted Turkmenistan's cooperation with
major US companies, including Nicklaus Companies, John Deere, Case
New Holland and Boeing.

The sides discussed political dialogue between their foreign
ministries and recent high-level contacts. These included
Berdimuhamedov's participation in the C5+1 summit in Washington in
November 2025 and the February 2026 visit to Florida by Gurbanguly
Berdimuhamedov, Chairman of the Halk Maslahaty.

According to the US Department of State, Landau's visit will
also include meetings with senior Turkmen officials and
representatives of the business communities of both countries.
Discussions are expected to focus on diversifying energy export
routes through the Trans-Caspian corridor, also known as the Middle
Corridor, and the Trump Route for International Peace and
Prosperity (TRIPP), as well as on opportunities to expand bilateral
trade and investment.

The TRIPP initiative, which is also expected to feature in the
discussions, stems from a US-brokered agreement between Azerbaijan
and Armenia. On August 8, 2025, following a trilateral meeting with
US President Donald Trump in Washington, Azerbaijani President
Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan signed a
joint declaration on establishing peace between Baku and Yerevan
and restoring transport connectivity between mainland Azerbaijan
and its Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic.

The proposed transit project was subsequently named the "Trump
Route for International Peace and Prosperity." During the same
meeting, Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and Armenian
Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan initialed the draft "Agreement on
the Establishment of Peace and Interstate Relations between the
Republic of Azerbaijan and the Republic of Armenia."

news.title: The Chinese internet is celebrating Jensen Huang’s triumphant return to power at Nvidia
news.text: It's a Jensen Huang party on the Chinese internet, and people are celebrating — and memeing — his return to Nvidia. Nvidia's board said Monday morning that Huang would return as the company's CEO, less than two weeks after he resigned. He made a jubilant speech at the Nvidia HQ on Monday, at which he apologized to his employees and promised to be a better CEO after his string of scandals, while surrounded by employees cheering his name. The same enthusiasm carried over to Weibo — a major Chinese social media platform similar to X — where people celebrated his return with teasing. As of press time, Huang-related topics accounted for three of Weibo's top five trending technology topics. "Jensen Huang makes a triumphant return after two weeks of unpaid leave," one Weibo user posting from the southern province of Hunan wrote. Another user from Jiangsu province in east China, calling out the fact that Huang's resignation period coincided with "GTA 6's" release, wrote, "Mystery solved: Jensen Huang quit his job to go home and play GTA 6. Now that he's had his fun, he's back at work." Others were quick to comment on his outfit. On his first day back at work, Huang had ditched his signature leather jacket, instead opting for a navy cotton one. Some Weibo users compared it to the jackets commonly worn by Chinese government officials, a style sometimes known as the "cadre look." But other users adopted a more serious, analytical tone. One user, posting from China's eastern Zhejiang province, wrote that Huang's return would benefit the AI industry but could lead to tighter restrictions on China's access to AI technology. Another user, posting from Shanxi province in northern China, wrote that Nvidia "cannot function without Huang," speculating that the company's manufacturing partners had pressured its board to bring him back because they feared a replacement CEO could disrupt their operations. It's not just the Chinese internet; Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia's CEO was a cause of celebration for many. Nvidia's stock rose more than 30% on Monday. Neocloud stocks rallied alongside it, with CoreWeave up 22% and Nebius up 20%. Asia's AI trade got a boost, too. Huang's allies in tech and politics rejoiced at the announcement. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, who last week offered Huang a job at the company after his ouster, wrote a triumphant "It is done" in an X post. President Donald Trump, who explicitly called for Huang's reinstatement in a Truth Social post on Sunday, wrote after the announcement that Nvidia's board had made the "correct and proper decision."
news.summary: From commenting on his makeover to memeing about "unpaid leave," the celebration on Weibo was mixed with a healthy dose of teasing.

news.title: Chinese stocks rebound from 16-month low as Nvidia comeback lifts AI shares
news.text:
SHANGHAI: Chinese stocks rebounded on Tuesday from a 16-month low as Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO sparked a rally in AI-related shares, helping reverse part of last week’s global equity selloff.

The move marks a sharp shift in sentiment after leadership turmoil at the world’s most valuable chipmaker and renewed concerns over AI spending rattled markets in recent sessions.

 The boost to Chinese and Hong Kong shares, however, was more subdued than in South Korea, Japan and the United States.

China’s blue-chip CSI300 Index gained 0.5%, while the Shanghai Composite Index rose 0.4%.

The 5G Communication Index rose as much as 7%.

Zhongji Innolight, an Nvidia supplier of optical transceivers, rose as much as 12% before paring some gains by midday.

“This is definitely a shot in the arm, as you can see from this morning’s trading,” said Zeng Wenkai, chief investment officer at Hong Kong-based Shengqi Capital.

“But A-shares and Hong Kong stocks follow their own patterns, independent of global markets, so it still comes down to how forcefully the ‘national team’ steps in to support the market this time,” he said, referring to China’s state-backed investors that buy stocks to stabilise markets.

The Shanghai Composite Index fell to its lowest since July 2025 on Monday before paring losses, as traders said state investors were buying some key index ETFs to lift the market. On Tuesday, the tech-focused STAR50 Index climbed 2.5%.

The CSI All Share Semiconductor Index rose 2.8%.

Memory-chip giant CXMT gained 2%.

China’s stocks have fallen more than 10% this year, braking a two-year rally that began when stimulus pledges sent shares soaring, and stalling Beijing’s efforts to break a long-standing boom-bust cycle in favour of a “slow bull” market that delivers steady returns. Regulators have also moved to shore up sentiment, with China’s three main exchanges announcing on Sunday a package of market-support measures, including easier margin-financing rules. Zeng Wanping, a fund manager at Beijing Monolith Fund Management, said Huang’s return would benefit Chinese firms in Nvidia’s supply chain, but the United States would not relax chip controls against China.

“Huang’s return was partly due to the Wall Street slump. It was not designed to rescue China’s stock market,” he said.

Hong Kong’s benchmark Hang Seng Index extended losses to its weakest level since April 2025, down 0.3%.

The Hang Seng Artificial Intelligence Index opened up 6% but reversed gains by midday.

“Huang’s return could revive hopes of a more pragmatic approach to US-China technology relations, particularly given his previous advocacy for access to the Chinese market,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo in Singapore.

“However, the political controversy surrounding his reinstatement could actually intensify scrutiny of Nvidia’s China exposure.

Export restrictions remain a structural constraint, regardless of who leads Nvidia.“

President Donald Trump said last week the US would penalise American companies that build data centers overseas, in Washington’s latest move to restrict Chinese access to advanced US chips.

Leading gains in Asia, South Korea’s KOSPI rose more than 6%, while Japan’s Nikkei gained nearly 4% by midday.

news.title: "Sex Sells, Fellas": Trump Reduces Nvidia Scandal To Locker Room Talk
news.text: Donald Trump, who became the first US president convicted of a crime when a jury found him guilty in May 2024 of falsifying records to hide a $130,000 payment to pornstar Stormy Daniels, has in a most obtuse manner characteristic of him alluded to the Jensen Huang episode as the fallout of wanton coverage despite the Nvidia boss having apologised for his indiscretion.The US president appeared to have suggested in a phone interview with CNBC that Jensen Huang's real misfortune was that he had "apologised" at all since, according to Trump, "that was what brought it to such a level, because sex sells, fellas".Huang got his job back last night after 11 days of uncertainty following his resignation and public apology over his extramarital affairs, chiefly with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman and former managing director of Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed International who faces US intelligence allegations of spying to steal AI technology for her country.In the world according to Trump, a corporate chief's sexual entanglement with a suspected foreign intelligence asset and a subordinate executive at his own firm could be seen as a marketing victory."I actually think it could be - I mean, it sounds strange - but I think it could be a net positive," Trump said.Many on social media noted that the US president's use of the word "fellas" also alluded to the conspiratorial wink of the boys' club and 'locker room' talk that reduced women to props in a spectacle that elevated the men who consumed them."I don't think he's (Jensen Huang) going to be diminished at all. I think people respect what he's gone through," Trump said, days after he waved off a counterintelligence probe against Alice Huang with a leer that "it was a pretty woman.""And any pretty woman that comes from China, they consider her to be a spy," he had said, dismissing workplace accountability as a minor lapse in "bad judgment" over "somewhat unrelated incidents".Trump had lobbied hard to get Huang his job back, since the alternative, according to him, would be China welcoming the AI industry veteran with open arms in what would be a loss for the US.The US president's excitement in seeing Huang return to Nvidia drove him to post on Truth Social an AI-tweaked version of a photo of him after he narrowly missed an assassination attempt in Pennsylvania during the 2024 presidential campaign.Trump replaced the image of him waving his fist in the air in triumph in that picture with a bloodied Jensen Huang holding up a red bra and Nvidia's logo swapped for the US flag in the background, flanked by Secret Service agents.People on social media highlighted that the post ridiculed the furore over Jensen Huang's affairs with Alice Huang and women working at Nvidia by turning a woman's undergarment into a battle trophy hoisted over a corporate logo, as if a red bra is the new colour of American technological supremacy.Trump himself has mostly remained tight-lipped about his connection with the disgraced sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The US president has never been formally accused of any wrongdoing relating to Epstein's crimes but a Wall Street Journal report had said he sent a lewd letter to the sex offender.Long before he became president, Trump, then a property mogul and self-styled playboy, knew Epstein since the 1990s. They partied together in 1992 with cheerleaders at Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida. The same year, Epstein was Trump's only guest at a "calendar girl" competition he hosted involving more than two dozen young women.

news.title: Singapore probe into Nvidia-linked Megaspeed following US trade blacklist
news.text: CANBERRA: Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong stated on November 24 that authorities will continue investigating cloud computing firm Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner added to the United States trade blacklist over allegations of diverting advanced AI chips to China, Reuters reported. Speaking at a joint press conference with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Canberra, Wong said Singapore is examining whether Megaspeed violated domestic regulations while remaining in contact with US officials. ."If there are companies that are caught breaching our laws, we will certainly take very firm enforcement actions. So it's on that basis that we were investigating Megaspeed," he stated, adding that while US investigations continue, Singapore’s inquiry focuses on potential breaches of local law.On November 23, the US Commerce Department placed Singapore-based Megaspeed on its trade blacklist, requiring the company to obtain Commerce Department approval, which is likely to be denied, before acquiring American exports.Megaspeed has faced US scrutiny since 2024 over suspected chip diversions to China, though the company maintained in a statement last week that it operates lawfully and complies with US export controls..In June 2025, US and Singaporean law enforcement conducted an on-site end-use inspection at Megaspeed and interviewed former CEO Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of ties to Beijing. Wong noted that Singapore previously investigated and released Alice Huang because "there was no basis for further prosecution."The enforcement action comes a day after Nvidia reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as chief executive following pressure from US President Donald Trump, reversing Huang’s recent resignation triggered by disclosures of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang.Separately, Singapore and Australia signed an agreement in Canberra on Tuesday to strengthen supply chains for essential goods, including food, pharmaceuticals, medical supplies, and agricultural inputs.(With inputs from agencies)

news.title: Jensen Huang’s return is a victory for visionary talent
news.text:
The share price had fallen too far. The clamour from the staff for his return was too great to ignore, the support from Donald Trump was ratcheting up the pressure, and none of the other potential candidates had anything like the same level of expertise. There were probably lots of reasons why the board of Nvidia, the chip giant, felt that it had no choice other than to bring back its chief executive Jensen Huang after ousting him a little over a week ago. And yet there was a larger explanation for his sensational comeback. A huge company can’t be run by committee, nor can trillions of dollars of assets be left at the mercy of politically correct corporate rules. Sure, Huang had his flaws, no one would deny that. But in the end, the company needed its visionary leader. 

Looking back, it is probably just as well that Jensen Huang never got around to updating his LinkedIn profile. Even as he was thrown out of the company he founded three decades ago, he maintained ‘Nvidia CEO’ on his profile, and in his only public comment on the matter quietly stated that he was ready to come back at any time. Meanwhile, both inside and outside the company, pressure was growing all the time. The ‘Stand With Jensen’ website already had 200,000 signatures by Monday morning for a petition to reinstall him, including 10,000 current Nvidians, as employees are known, and 100,000 shareholders. Leading tech industry figures such as Elon Musk had thrown their support behind him, and on Sunday, so did the President, who described him as ‘one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world’, adding that he would ‘love to see Jensen be given a second chance.’ 

With the stock down by almost 30 per cent since his departure, and with the entire artificial intelligence boom that has propped up Wall Street and the American economy starting to unravel, the board succumbed to that pressure, reinstating their former CEO, after, it said, receiving reassurance from the American government that he posed ‘no threat to national security.’ Less than two weeks after he was fired, Jensen was back. 

That is probably the right outcome. In the wake of his departure, it was already clear that the board had acted too hastily. For all the allegations thrown around, it was far from clear that Huang was really guilty of anything other than breaking his marriage vows. It was not proved that his Chinese mistress, Alice Huang (no relation), was really a ‘honeypot agent’ of the Chinese government, while the second affair, this one with a senior Nvidia executive, may have broken company rules, but was completely consensual. Huang may have acted foolishly. But he had also built Nvidia from nothing and turned it into the world’s largest company, as well as the driving force behind America’s huge global lead in AI. Given that none of the other potential candidates, either internal or external, had anything like the same level of knowledge or ability, bringing him back was the only realistic option. Even worse, an open civil war would have crippled the business. 

In the wake of the CEO’s return, two points are now clear. To start with, Huang will be more powerful than ever. He may only own 4 per cent of the stock, but he has just proved how completely indispensable he is to its future. The Nvidians who didn’t sign the ‘Stand With Jensen’ petition must be feeling, to put it mildly, a little uncomfortable by now, while the position of the board, after making such a mess of the whole process, is surely untenable. The chairman Harvey C. Jones will have to be replaced, and so will most of the other non-executives. Within the company, Huang’s authority will be total.
