news.title: Huang returns as Nvidia CEO after Trump intervention in abrupt board reversal
news.text:
Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday under pressure from US President Donald Trump, a stunning reversal following his resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, drawing approval from Wall Street and opposition from US lawmakers.

Huang’s comeback caps a whirlwind week of events that roiled markets and tore through the AI ecosystem that has relied on Nvidia for everything from supplying chips to bankrolling the industry’s massive buildout.

But the board’s about-face — less than a week after Chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia would not rehire Huang as CEO because his personal behavior was inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct — raises questions about its independence, governance experts said, even as the company’s investigation remains unfinished.

Huang’s comeback boosted Wall Street and sent Nvidia’s shares soaring. The stock closed up 31.5%, adding nearly $1 trillion in market value, vaulting the chipmaker back to the position of the second-biggest company by market value after Apple.

The gains were not enough, however, to erase all losses since Huang’s resignation on November 12.

Nvidia said in a statement that based on US government input the board was confident that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” a claim backed by Trump in an interview with CNBC.

Huang said in a statement that he was honored to return and “can’t wait to get back to work.”

He returned to company headquarters to cheers from employees.

“Jensen’s return is not a total shock, but it does send a troubling message about the state of corporate governance in America,” said James St. Aubin, chief investment officer at Ocean Park Asset Management.

“Certain executives are going to be held to different standards if you are perceived to be a one of one,” he said, adding Huang would still have to answer “some tough questions from Congress.”

Lawmakers across party lines strongly objected to Huang’s reinstatement and called on Congress to pass the Chip Security Act, a bill that seeks to stop legally exported advanced chips from being diverted to China, where their sales are restricted.

US Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Trump was “putting his own financial interests before our national security,” while Senator Pete Ricketts, a Nebraska Republican, said Huang’s return “doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips.” 

Trump’s support for Huang

Huang returned at the strong urging of Trump, industry leaders including Elon Musk, and some investors.

His departure had reverberated from Silicon Valley to Taipei.

A petition calling for his reinstatement drew more than 180,000 signatures, underscoring the unusually strong support for an executive who stepped down amid controversy.

“I believe my intervention was very important to get Jensen Huang back,” Trump told CNBC. Trump owns between $11 million and $55 million in Nvidia stock, according to a Reuters review of his annual financial disclosure for 2025 and share trading disclosures for 2026. Monday’s surge in Nvidia shares could have boosted Trump’s net worth by as much as $17 million.

A White House spokesperson said Trump’s stock and bond portfolio was independently managed by third-party financial institutions and neither the president nor any member of his family had any ability to direct or influence how the portfolio was invested.

Nvidia’s board did not mention Huang’s affairs.

Apart from Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman who is accused of having ties with Beijing, Huang is accused of having had intimate relationships with at least two Nvidia employees.

Jensen Huang has acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologized, but has not publicly addressed the individual alleged relationships in detail.

China has denied the espionage allegations.

Attempts by Reuters to reach Alice Huang have been unsuccessful. China is key to Nvidia

Huang’s return comes as Nvidia faces heightened scrutiny in Washington over the flow of advanced AI chips to China.

US authorities have tightened licensing rules for some chip shipments and overseas data centers serving Chinese companies, while lawmakers are preparing to question Huang, who has pushed for greater access to the Chinese market.

Huang has agreed to testify before the US Senate in a public hearing on December 3, the Senate Banking Committee said.

Huang’s personal spokesperson declined to comment.

Trump told CNBC that he had urged Nvidia to continue reviewing its compliance with US export controls to ensure it was adequately protecting national security.

Trump, who visited Shenzhen last week, said he had spoken to Chinese President Xi Jinping about Huang. Huang’s exit from Nvidia threatened its business in China, Reuters reported on Monday, with some customers there cancelling or hesitating to place orders, jeopardizing billions in revenue.

The US on Monday added Alice Huang’s former employer Megaspeed and Alibaba’s Singapore subsidiary, which has business ties to the cloud firm at the center of the Nvidia scandal, to its trade blacklist.

Alibaba said allegations the subsidiary had diverted chips subject to US export restrictions were “erroneous,” while Megaspeed has previously said it conducted legitimate and lawful business, including complying with US export controls.

Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said on Tuesday the city-state would continue its investigation into Megaspeed. US and Singapore law enforcement conducted an onsite visit in 2025 and interviewed Alice Huang.

The Nvidia board has formed a committee to investigate whether foreign intelligence efforts targeted Huang and another committee focused on national security and export controls.

The company is also facing multiple investigations over issues ranging from potential accounting irregularities to suspected chip smuggling, and a shareholder lawsuit accusing the company and Huang of defrauding shareholders by concealing Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang.

news.title: US flew drone over Mexican territory to help capture drug lord in Sinaloa
news.text:
MEXICO CITY -- The United States flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to help the government track down and capture a top drug lord over the weekend in Sinaloa, Mexican security officials said Monday.

The recent detention of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro” illustrates increasing law enforcement cooperation between the neighboring countries, but U.S. involvement in Mexican security operations has long been a touchy subject.

U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to crack down on cartels, while Mexico has repeatedly underscored its sovereignty. On Monday, Sheinbaum emphasized that U.S. forces were not allowed to operate on the ground in Mexico and the governments were only sharing intelligence.

“This case in particular demonstrates the capacity of the armed forces” of Mexico to make major detentions, Sheinbaum said.

The U.S. has sought to line up allies across Latin America to allow U.S. forces to operate in their territories, with mixed responses from across the region.

The weekend detention of the capo, who was one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives, triggered a burst of violence in the northern state of Sinaloa that left 20 people dead in the city of Guasave. Among them were four soldiers and 16 suspected criminals, Mexican officials said Monday.

Defense Secretary Gen. Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said Monday that the capture of Meza Flores and 16 members of his criminal group was the result of “very important intelligence sharing” with U.S. authorities over the past three months to pinpoint Meza Flores’ location in Guasave.

In the week leading up to Meza Flores’ capture, that included authorizing the U.S. to fly intelligence drones over Mexican territory to assist Mexican law enforcement to later surround the capo and go in for the capture, Trevilla Trejo and other Mexican officials said. They emphasized that the intelligence mission was carried out in compliance with Mexican law.

On Monday, Mexico's prosecutors' office announced that it had formally charged Meza Flores and two other alleged cartel members with illegal possession of firearms and possession of methamphetamine with the intent to sell, adding that the three were flown to Mexico City over the weekend following their capture.

Authorities also highlighted that the U.S. has an existing extradition request for Meza Flores for drug trafficking charges, leaving open the possibility that the cartel boss may be sent north to face justice.

His capture was celebrated by Mexican and U.S. law enforcement as a major blow to criminal groups in the region. 

The U.S. government highlighted its intelligence support in the operation, but did not immediately provide more details about the use of the surveillance drone when asked on Monday.

Meza Flores led the Beltran Leyva organization and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. He was also a key ally of a Sinaloa Cartel faction known as “Los Mayos," which is locked in a brutal territorial war against another cartel faction in the Mexican state.

The capture of Meza Flores was the latest in a string of targeted operations against cartel kingpins by Mexican authorities, the largest of which was the February killing of Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as " El Mencho." 

While the captures show that the government is doubling down on its fight against crime, many experts were quick to emphasize that the strategy could backfire. 

In previous anti-crime offensives in Mexico and other parts of Latin America, knocking out cartel leaders without debilitating the entire criminal structure around them has largely only fueled bloody power struggles between cartel factions. That has been the case in recent years in Sinaloa.
news.summary: Mexican security officials say the United States flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to help the government track down and capture a top drug lord over the weekend in Sinaloa

news.title: Meet the major players in Spain's general election
news.text:
BARCELONA, Spain -- Spaniards will vote in a general election Sunday, with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez seeking to fend off conservative and far-right challengers to earn yet another term.

Sánchez’s main rival is conservative Alberto Núñez Feijóo, while the far-right’s Santiago Abascal is vying to play kingmaker to Núñez Feijóo and usher in a right-wing coalition.

Here's what you need to know about the top candidates.

Pedro Sánchez of the Socialist Party has led Spain’s government since 2018, making him one of Europe’s longest-serving leaders.

With his polished appearance and command of English, Sánchez has become a darling of the global progressive movement.

He has staked out strong positions against U.S. President Donald Trump and the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, as well as Israel’s military operations in Gaza. He has remained firm on his pro-migration policies amid a wider anti-immigration mood sweeping the developed world. He has overseen Europe's fastest growing major economy for several years, but greater wealth has not helped extinguish anger over rising housing costs.

Sánchez, 54, is a fierce campaigner who has outwitted adversaries both inside and outside his party and repeatedly beaten the odds, earning him the reputation of a political escape artist.

The most recent example of his electoral savvy came in 2023 when Sánchez’s Socialist Party took a beating in regional elections. Instead of licking his wounds, the very next day he stunned the country by calling for a general election, and he campaigned on fears of the far right entering government. The audacious move worked, and voters let him stay in office after forming another left-wing coalition.

Now the trained economist arguably faces his greatest challenge. He is dogged by legal cases involving corruption by a former minister and top officials in his party as well as his wife — who denies wrongdoing.

Sánchez’s fate will most likely depend not only on his Socialists rallying but also a group of smaller parties to the Left outperforming polling that predicts they will lose votes.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the Popular Party is a lifelong civil servant-turned-politician who has avoided scandal and projects himself as a sensible, moderate and effective center-right administrator.

Known nationally by his second last name, Feijóo won election after election in Galicia during the 13 years in which he governed the rural northwest corner of Spain. Despite being a less-developed region, Galicia has a long tradition of producing strong politicians. Among them were 20th-century dictator Francisco Franco and former Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy, who ran Spain from 2011 until 2018 — the last time the Popular Party led Spain.

Feijóo, 65, wants to reduce government regulations and lower taxes while, like Sánchez, is staunchly pro-European Union. If he wins, Feijóo is expected to mend bridges with the U.S. and Israel.

Feijóo made the leap to take over his party in time to lead it during the previous general election, when he failed to oust Sánchez.

That means the pressure is on Feijóo to make good on the broad support the Popular Party has maintained since then. 

While the low-key Feijóo may be overshadowed by his rivals, he is in charge of the Popular Party's finely tuned vote-winning machine that's entrenched in the capital, Madrid, as well as many of Spain's rural provinces.

Bearded and barrel-chested in his tailored suits, Santiago Abascal is a member of the global populist right who exudes macho toughness, and his candidacy could ensure Feijóo has a coalition to govern.

Abascal, 50, is from Spain’s northern Basque Country. Like many politicians from across the spectrum in Spain, his ultranationalist ideology was shaped in response to the violence of the region’s separatist group ETA, which disbanded in 2018.

The first part of Abascal’s political career was as a rank-and-file member of the Popular Party before he and others splintered off to found Vox in late 2013. He quickly took over as its leader and has maintained firm control of the party ever since.

His ideology fits within the wider populist right movement, from the U.S. to Europe. He is a staunch defender of Israel and has strongly criticized Spain's position under Sánchez toward the country. He wants to slash government regulations for business and cut taxes, and is an open admirer of Argentina's chainsaw-wielding President Javier Milei.

Like Milei, Abascal slams progressive causes, including feminist thought, while dismissing climate change. Vox is not openly hostile to the EU, unlike other far-right European parties, but he blames immigration for Spain’s cost-of-living pains.

Far-right parties like Vox have been boxed out of government in Spain since the return of democracy following Franco's death in 1975. After losing seats in the 2023 election, Vox is aiming for a rebound that would afford it the leverage to demand ministries as a junior member in what Abascal hopes will be Feijóo's triumphal government.

Right-wing voters who find Vox too mild can opt for “Se Acabó la Fiesta" (The Party Is Over), the political vehicle of a far-right social media influencer.

On the other end of the spectrum, in-fighting impeded smaller progressive parties from remaking an electoral coalition that helped the left stay in power in 2023. This time, the Frente Amplio (Broad Front) will compete with Podemos (We Can) for the most left-leaning of voters. That will hurt both their prospects, as well as Sánchez's shot at forming another left-wing coalition.

There are also traditional parties that focus on influencing how policies and laws impact their home territories. These regionalist parties in Catalonia, the Basque Country, Galicia and the Canary Islands could play a role in forming a ruling coalition if the results are close.
news.summary: Spaniards will vote in a general election Sunday, when Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will try to defy the polls that point to a combined victory for conservative and far-right challengers

news.title: Massachusetts sues Trump admin to stop ICE's courthouse arrests: 'Unnecessary fear'
news.text: Massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration on Monday to block Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from carrying out civil arrests in the state's courthouses, arguing that such arrests without judicial warrants are illegal under state law. The lawsuit filed by Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell challenges a 2025 ICE directive that authorizes agents to conduct civil arrests in or near state courthouses without judicial warrants, which she says violates the PROTECT Act, a new state law passed ​by the Democratic-led legislature that prohibits civil immigration arrests in state courthouses without judicial warrants. The courthouse protections took effect Nov. 3. Campbell said the ICE directive interferes with the state's authority to operate its judicial system, disrupts court proceedings, undermines constitutional principles and public safety and spreads fear, chaos and confusion. "The Massachusetts PROTECT Act makes it illegal for ICE to conduct civil arrests in our courthouses without a judicial warrant. ICE’s intentional violation of state law has created unnecessary fear, made it more difficult to operate our courts and hold defendants accountable," Campbell said in a statement. DOJ SUES TO STOP OHIO COURT BLOCKING COURTHOUSE ARRESTS "ICE is misleading the public by suggesting that these arrests make us safer when, in fact, ICE's actions are preventing criminal cases from moving forward, denying a victim’s ability to obtain accountability, violating a defendant’s due process, and leaving open the possibility that someone facing serious criminal charges could ultimately be released from ICE custody without their criminal case ever being resolved," she continued. The attorney general said more than 1,110 people have been arrested at her state's courthouses since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, including more than 600 people in 2025 and more than 500 during the first 10 months of 2026. Campbell said ICE has ignored the new state law and arrested at least 38 people in Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants in the two and a half weeks since the courthouse protections went into effect. "I, along with our district attorneys, share the goal of holding defendants accountable for crimes, yet ICE’s unlawful tactics to arrest someone for a civil immigration violation is not the same as holding them accountable for a crime," Campbell said. FEDERAL JUDGE IN NEW YORK TIES TRUMP ADMIN HANDS ON ARRESTS AT IMMIGRATION COURTS Campbell said that ICE's courthouse arrests have continued in Massachusetts despite a federal ruling handed down in June by U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts in California that vacated the Trump administration's courthouse arrest policy ​in a separate class action lawsuit. In Monday's lawsuit, Campbell argues the ICE policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act since it was adopted without taking into account the impact it would have on states and because the Immigration and Nationality Act does not explicitly authorize courthouse arrests. The lawsuit also alleges that the ⁠policy violates the U.S. Constitution's Tenth Amendment, which protects states' rights to maintain authority over their own judicial systems. "The Trump Administration’s ICE arrests at Massachusetts courthouses are interfering with our justice system and undermining public safety. When people are afraid to go to court, victims are less likely to report crimes, survivors are less likely to seek protection, and our communities are less safe," Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey said in a statement. "We expect ICE and all federal agents to follow Massachusetts law." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment. In a statement to Reuters, a DHS spokesperson argued that making immigration arrests at courthouses "conserves valuable law enforcement resources because they already ​know where a target will ​be," adding that "the ability of law enforcement ⁠to make arrests of criminal illegal aliens in courthouses is common sense." A similar lawsuit against ICE arrests at state courthouses was filed in October by California Attorney General Rob Bonta.
news.summary: Massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration over ICE's courthouse arrests without judicial warrants, saying they violate a new state law.

news.title: The Directors Who Put Jensen Huang Back In Charge Of Nvidia
news.text: After the shocking ouster and return of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang this month, the chipmaker's board of directors is facing growing scrutiny. Nvidia's directors had long stayed in relative obscurity, even as the company grew into a chip colossus and the top beneficiary of the AI spending boom. But a scandal involving Huang's extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China, thrust the board into the spotlight.After cutting ties with Huang less than two weeks ago, the directors just voted unanimously to reinstate him as president and CEO. The company said the board held a series of meetings with Huang and received input from the US government before making its decision. Separately, US President Donald Trump claimed credit for Huang's return, saying he'd intervened with the Santa Clara, California-based company.Nvidia's directors have a variety of backgrounds, ranging from running Taco Bell's international operations to academic research involving a jellyfish. Huang has known many of them for decades.The group scored near the bottom of an annual assessment that ranks the governance of companies in the S&P 500 and Fortune 500. The ranking by US executive recruiting company James Drury Partners put it in 609th place, out of more than 650 companies, lower than its biggest tech peers.Here's a look at the people who presided over Huang's dramatic comeback:Harvey C. JonesNamed Nvidia's chairman earlier this month, Harvey C. Jones joined Nvidia's board in 1993. At the time, he was serving as CEO of chip-design software maker Synopsys Inc. Since 2004, he has been managing partner at private investment firm Square Wave Ventures. He holds degrees from Georgetown University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Last year, Nvidia bought a $2 billion stake in Synopsys.Stephen C. NealNeal joined the Nvidia board in 2019 and brings extensive legal experience to the role. He is chairman emeritus and senior counsel at Cooley LLP, Nvidia's longtime law firm. He has degrees from Harvard University and Stanford Law School.Tench CoxeCoxe, a billionaire and longtime Silicon Valley venture capitalist, has been on the Nvidia board since 1993. He was a managing director at Palo Alto-based Sutter Hill Ventures from 1989 to 2020, and was an early investor in Nvidia. He and his wife live in Austin, Texas, where they've become active political donors and local investors. In January, Coxe donated $100 million from his fortune to help launch a medical center at the University of Texas at Austin.John O. DabiriA board member since 2020, Dabiri is a decorated academic who has received a National Medal of Science and funding from the MacArthur Foundation. He is a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology.As an undergraduate at Princeton, he used videos of jellyfish taken at an aquarium to write mathematical models that describe their movement.Dawn HudsonHudson has been on Nvidia's board since 2013. She was earlier chief marketing officer of the National Football League and before that CEO of Pepsi-Cola North America.Photo Credit: BloombergMelissa B. LoraLora is a relative newcomer to the board, having joined in 2023. Before that she was president of Taco Bell International. In an announcement when she joined, Huang hailed her "extensive finance expertise." She has degrees from California State University Long Beach and the University of Southern California.A. Brooke SeawellAnother long-standing board member, Seawell joined the board in 1997, just four years after Nvidia's founding. He is a partner at venture capital firm New Enterprise Associates. Earlier he was an executive at NetDynamics Inc., an application server software company that Sun Microsystems Inc. acquired. He also previously worked at Synopsys. He has degrees from Stanford University.Aarti ShahShah worked at pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly & Co. for 27 years, where she was senior vice president and chief information and digital officer. When she joined Nvidia's board in 2020, Huang deemed her "a world-class leader." She has a Ph.D. in applied statistics from the University of California, Riverside.Mark A. StevensStevens served on Nvidia's board from 1993 to 2006, before rejoining in 2008. He is managing partner at private family office investment firm S-Cubed Capital and was an early investor in Nvidia. Previously, he was managing partner at venture capital firm Sequoia Capital. He has an MBA from Harvard Business School.Suzanne Nora JohnsonNora Johnson joined the board in July, making her its newest addition. She spent 21 years at Goldman Sachs Group Inc., where she was vice chairman. "Suzanne is an extraordinary leader whose career spans finance, technology, healthcare and public policy," Huang said at the time. She has degrees from the University of Southern California and Harvard Law School. (Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: How Donald Trump ensured Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO
news.text:
Jensen Huang is Nvidia's chief executive again. The company's board voted unanimously on Monday to reinstate him as president, CEO and director, effective immediately.
The announcement came 11 days after he resigned amid a scandal over an extramarital affair, and a few days after the board publicly said it would not take him back.
United States President Donald Trump says his own intervention made the difference.
The reversal has also set off a new round of bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, with hearings now scheduled for next week.
What Nvidia announced
In its filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Nvidia said the board was satisfied with Huang's candour and ability to lead after a series of meetings with him.
It also said the board received input from senior levels of the US government and, based on that input, is confident his reinstatement poses no national security risk.
Board Chairman Harvey C Jones said the board believes Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia and that his return serves stockholders, employees, partners and customers. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who had served as interim CEO, returns to her role as CFO.
Huang said in a statement that he was honoured to return and takes up the role "with the greatest humility and renewed commitment." Employees gathered in the atrium at the Silicon Valley headquarters and cheered him loudly.
Huang told them he would be a better CEO the second time around.
How Trump engineered the return
The Washington Post reported that Trump personally orchestrated the effort over several days, an extraordinary intervention in a private company. Top officials led by Vice President JD Vance privately leaned on the board in a flurry of weekend calls.
A person familiar with the matter told the AP that the White House believed Vance, who worked in Silicon Valley before entering politics, had the stature to ease board members' reservations.
Trump confirmed his role in a long phone interview with CNBC. He said he spoke with the board "directly and indirectly," a highly unusual step for a US president. CNBC's sources said the decision was sealed on Sunday by a personal promise from Trump that Huang had not broken national security laws.
Trump said the board had asked for guarantees on that point. Trump declined to say whether he called into the board meeting, but said he was effectively "represented" there. He also said the board "decided to do what we wanted them to do."
Trump named Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick as the officials he worked with. US Attorney General Todd Blanche, Trump said, confirmed that the government has no evidence Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.
The administration was not unified on Huang. Bessent had earlier called on Fox News for a "dramatic shake-up" at Nvidia and said the next CEO should come from outside the company. By the weekend he had softened his position.
He called the focus on the affair "kind of a canard" and said the administration's real concern was corporate governance. Bessent told CBS on Sunday that Huang was "on the outside now."
Why Trump says he did it
Trump gave several reasons. He told PBS News that a federal review had found Huang showed bad judgement in "somewhat unrelated incidents" but did nothing wrong.
He argued the real danger lay elsewhere. Losing the brainpower of someone like Huang would be a far bigger threat, Trump said, and he voiced concern that China could recruit him. He also said there is "nothing wrong with a comeback."
He also acknowledged the market. Trump said last week's stock declines, one of the worst weeks since the 2008 financial crisis, "probably" influenced his thinking.
A source told CNN that Trump insisted Huang had to return to help steady the market. In a social media post, Trump said the country "needs Jensen's leadership" for the success of both the company and the American economy.
Trump and Huang have a long, close relationship. Huang is close to Trump, who has hosted him at the White House and on Air Force One and awarded him a National Medal of Science.
In January, Huang won Trump's approval to sell Nvidia's H200 chips to China. Huang has also been public about it.
At an Nvidia conference in Washington, he said Trump's late-evening phone calls to him were always about making America rich, and confirmed Nvidia donated to Trump's ballroom project.
How Huang fell in under two weeks
The fall was fast. The New York Times reported that Huang had a relationship with a woman US officials had concluded was a Chinese spy, recruited to influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available in China.
The woman is Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International. The two are not related. China has denied trying to ensnare Huang. Blanche has said the Justice Department has not reached a conclusion on whether she is a spy.
Pressure built quickly. Nvidia's board announced an investigation on a Sunday while saying it still had confidence in Huang. Late that Wednesday, reports surfaced of another alleged affair, this time with an Nvidia employee who reported to him.
Huang had told employees he was unfaithful to his wife, adding "There is no excuse for what I did."
Huang resigned on Thursday, November 12. Shares fell 14 per cent at the opening bell before stabilizing and closed down about 4 per cent.
Kress was named interim CEO, and the board named its first-ever chairman, Jones. Nvidia had no succession plan. The board reportedly sought out Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas as a possible successor.
A "Stand with Jensen" petition began circulating. It drew signatures from current and former Nvidia staff, investors and Silicon Valley figures including Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.
Its organisers questioned whether Alice Huang was a spy and argued Huang was removed without due process.
On November 16, Trump said Huang "learned a big lesson" and he "would certainly not mind" seeing him reinstated. He also said no one had proven the woman was a spy. Nvidia's stock fell 4.1 per cent that day, and the S&P 500 lost nearly 2 per cent.
The next day, Huang posted that he would be "honoured" to return if the board decided it was best for shareholders, employees, the company and the country. He acknowledged "serious mistakes" in his personal life.
Jones said the same day the board did not intend to reinstate him. By Monday, that position had reversed.
How Wall Street reacted
The market response was dramatic. Nvidia closed up 31.48 per cent, its best day since 2003, a gain of about $952 billion in market value. MarketWatch called that the biggest single-day market-value gain for any US stock. Short sellers and inverse Nvidia products took heavy losses.
The rally spread. The S&P 500 rose 4.7 per cent to 7,237, the Nasdaq 6.5 per cent to 24,089 and the Dow 3.0 per cent to 49,595 with the Nasdaq-100 adding more than $2 trillion in market value.
CoreWeave shares jumped 22 per cent. Tech stocks across Asia also rose Tuesday. That $2 trillion figure covers the whole index, not Nvidia alone.
The recovery is partial. Nvidia fell nearly 23 per cent last week and is still below where it traded before the scandal broke. The stock reached an all-time high of $239.24 last month. Before Monday, a 1 per cent move in Nvidia affected the S&P 500 more than a 1 per cent move in all but two other index members.
TradeStation's David Russell said never has so much value rested on one executive.
Analyst Dan Ives kept his Outperform rating and $225 price target but said the higher valuation depends on resolving the investigations and governance questions, not on Huang's return alone.
How US Congress has reacted
US Senator Tim Scott, the outgoing Republican chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, announced Huang will testify publicly on December 3. Senator Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair, called the decision "reckless" and said the administration must explain what role US officials played.
Democrats were sharply critical. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries called the decision "indefensible, irresponsible, and incomprehensible."
Rep Robert Garcia, the incoming House oversight chairman, said Trump's direct involvement raises serious national security and corruption questions. Senator Ron Wyden said it shows that "our national security is for sale."
Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress should look at what stock positions were taken before the announcement.
Several Republicans also objected, mostly those leaving Congress. Senator John Cornyn asked on what basis officials concluded there was no national security risk, and whether the FBI had given Huang a defensive briefing.
Senator John Curtis asked who in government weighed in and what they told the board. Rep Don Bacon said Congress must find out who approved high-end chip sales to China.
Senator Tom Cotton, the Republican chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said the Nvidia-Megaspeed controversy is "the tip of the iceberg" and is not resolved. Cotton also said Congress will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export control bills.
What about Lutnick
Democrats preparing to take committee gavels in January are focusing on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Bessent said earlier this month he was frustrated by Commerce's delay in restricting Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed.
House Democrats have written to Lutnick's son, who chairs Cantor Fitzgerald, alleging Lutnick resisted tougher action on suspected chip diversion. Cantor called the claims "baseless." Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, though no date has been set.
Many have also raised other connections. Yale's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld noted that Trump's portfolio holds Nvidia stock, which the Washington Post reported may have exceeded $60 million in August, and that Lutnick's sons' investment bank does business with Nvidia customers.
Others pointed to Nvidia's $25 million contribution to the White House ballroom project. The White House has not answered questions about those ties.
What next for Nvidia
The company says it is making changes. An independent-director committee, advised by outside counsel, is investigating reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
The board said that probe will continue to its conclusion. A separate National Security and Export Control Committee, made up solely of independent directors, will oversee trade compliance and national security risks.
Nvidia is also searching for a new Chief Compliance Officer who will report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. The company says it will keep cooperating with government investigations.
Trump also called for the internal investigation to continue. Its findings have not been made public.
The reinstatement settles who leads Nvidia, not the underlying questions. It does not end the congressional probes into the affair and the suspected diversion of advanced chips to China.
The US Justice Department is conducting a criminal investigation into potential export control violations at Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was an executive. Megaspeed has said it cooperated with the Commerce Department's export enforcement bureau and hired a US law firm to take a census of its chips.
Singapore authorities questioned Alice Huang last year, concluded there was not enough evidence of a crime, and barred her from returning.
A proposed class action accuses Nvidia and Huang of misleading investors about his relationship with Alice Huang and its national security implications. A separate derivative suit accuses directors of ignoring warning signs. The allegations are unproven.
Senators Warren and Jim Banks have said Nvidia reportedly received approvals to export hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China's military.
Huang is due to give a closed-door transcribed interview to three House committees on December 1.
Those panels are the House Intelligence Committee, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. Nvidia's general counsel is also expected to appear.
On December 3, Huang is scheduled to appear in public before the Senate Banking Committee at a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls."
Democrats take control of Congress in January and are expected to open broader investigations.
With inputs from agencies

news.title: Friendship Files: How Trump and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang grew closer
news.text:
Jensen Huang’s journey to the top of the global technology industry began far from Silicon Valley.
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang moved to Thailand with his family when he was young. At the age of nine, he and his older brother were sent to the United States. They initially stayed with an uncle in Tacoma, Washington, before being enrolled at the Oneida Baptist Institute in Kentucky.
The transition was difficult. As Stephen Witt writes in his book The Thinking Machine, Huang has spoken about the challenges of adjusting to life in the US and the tough environment at the boarding school. He has also recalled doing chores, including cleaning bathrooms.
Those early years were followed by an education in engineering. Huang studied electrical engineering at Oregon State University and later earned a master's degree from Stanford University. He worked at chipmakers AMD and LSI Logic before setting out on his own.
In 1993, Huang co-founded Nvidia with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. The company initially focused on graphics chips for computers and video games. Its fortunes changed as graphics processing units, or GPUs, became central to artificial intelligence and high-performance computing.
The launch of CUDA in 2006 allowed developers to use Nvidia GPUs for a much wider range of computing tasks. Few could have predicted that nearly two decades later, the technology would put Nvidia at the centre of the global AI boom.
By the time Huang began interacting with Donald Trump during his second presidency, Nvidia had become one of the most consequential companies in the technology industry. Its chips were powering the AI race, while Washington was increasingly focused on controlling China's access to advanced semiconductors.
The relationship between the two men would develop against this backdrop of technology, trade, national security and business.
January 2025: The first meeting
13 January 2025: Nvidia contributed $1 million to Donald Trump's inaugural fund, according to campaign finance records. The donation came days before Trump returned to the White House.
29 January 2025: Trump's financial disclosures later showed that accounts associated with him had purchased between $1 million and $5 million worth of Nvidia shares. The transaction was reported two days before his first Oval Office meeting with Huang.
The White House has said that independent financial institutions manage his portfolio without input from the president or his family.
31 January 2025: Huang met Trump at the White House for the first time during his second term. The meeting came as the administration was reviewing US restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports to China.
The interaction was not immediately a sign of a close relationship. A New York Times report later described the first meeting as awkward, with the two struggling to connect.
Huang was seeking to make the case for Nvidia's position in the China market. Trump, meanwhile, was weighing how to balance US technological leadership with concerns about China's access to advanced chips.
April 2025: The China chip restrictions
The relationship faced an early test in April, when the Trump administration restricted Nvidia's H20 chip sales to China.
The H20 was designed to comply with earlier US export restrictions. The new licensing requirement threatened to disrupt Nvidia's business in one of its most important markets.
For Huang, the decision was a major concern. He had repeatedly argued that US companies should be allowed to compete in China rather than leave the market to domestic rivals.
On 14 April, Nvidia announced plans to build and produce AI infrastructure worth up to $500 billion in the United States over four years. The plan included manufacturing and supply-chain commitments involving partners.
Huang's presence alongside Trump at a White House event later that month underscored Nvidia's growing importance to the administration's domestic AI ambitions.
The announcement also gave the two sides a significant area of common ground. Trump wanted to expand US manufacturing and maintain American leadership in AI. Huang wanted a supportive policy environment for Nvidia's expansion.
May 2025: Huang joins Trump in Saudi Arabia
Huang's role began extending beyond Washington.
In May, he accompanied Trump on the US president's trip to Saudi Arabia. The visit was part of a wider push to deepen economic and technology ties between Washington and Gulf countries.
Nvidia was among the companies looking to benefit from the region's growing demand for AI infrastructure. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates were seeking access to advanced chips and computing capacity to build their own AI industries.
Huang was also becoming a familiar presence around Trump. The Nvidia chief had moved from a difficult first meeting with the president to accompanying him on an important international visit.
July and August 2025: A breakthrough on H20 sales
The biggest policy breakthrough for Nvidia came in the summer.
14 July 2025: Nvidia said it had applied for licences to resume H20 sales to China. The move followed discussions with the Trump administration.
16 July 2025: Huang spoke in Beijing about the company's efforts to increase supplies of H20 chips to China. The developments suggested that Washington was prepared to reconsider its earlier restrictions.
August 2025: The Trump administration agreed to allow Nvidia to resume H20 sales under a revenue-sharing arrangement. The company would pay the US government 15 per cent of revenue from the approved sales.
Trump later said he had initially sought a 20 per cent share, but the figure was negotiated down to 15 per cent.
The arrangement was unusual. It linked export permissions to a direct payment to the US government and showed how chip sales had become part of the administration's trade and economic strategy.
For Huang, it offered a route back into the Chinese market, although the arrangement did not remove the wider uncertainty surrounding US export controls.
Trump's financial disclosures also showed that accounts associated with him purchased between $5 million and $25 million worth of Nvidia shares in August.
September and October 2025: From policy talks to public gestures
 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang arrive to attend the State Banquet during US President Donald Trump's state visit, at Windsor Castle, in Windsor, Britain, September 17, 2025. File/Reuters
September 2025: Huang accompanied Trump on his visit to the United Kingdom. The trip included meetings with business leaders and discussions around technology and investment.
Nvidia's growing role in the AI industry made Huang an important figure in the administration's international technology outreach.
October 2025: Huang presented Trump with a silicon wafer containing chips manufactured in Arizona. The gesture highlighted Nvidia's US manufacturing plans and the administration's push to strengthen domestic semiconductor production.
It was also a visible symbol of the growing familiarity between the two men.
November 2025: Trump publicly praised Huang during an appearance at an international summit in South Korea, referring to him as "my friend".
The remark reflected how far their public relationship had moved since the first Oval Office meeting in January.
A New York Times report in November 2025 described Huang as an increasingly regular companion on Trump's international travels. It also highlighted the growing overlap between Nvidia's commercial ambitions and the administration's diplomatic agenda.
December 2025: A new opening for Nvidia in China
8 December 2025: Trump announced that the US would allow Nvidia to sell its more advanced H200 AI chips to approved customers in China.
The arrangement came with a condition. The US government would receive 25 per cent of the revenue from the approved sales.
The H200 decision was separate from the earlier H20 arrangement, which involved a 15 per cent revenue share.
The move was significant for Nvidia. China remained a large potential market for the company, even as Washington continued to restrict access to its most advanced technology.
By the end of 2025, financial disclosures showed that Trump's Nvidia holdings had risen substantially. Accounts associated with the president held Nvidia shares valued in a range of $12.5 million to $58 million, compared with between $615,000 and $1.3 million a year earlier.
(These figures represent disclosed value ranges, not confirmed profits. The disclosures also do not establish that Trump directed the transactions.)
2026: The relationship faces a national security test
The following year brought a more complicated turn.
Trump's financial disclosures showed that accounts associated with him made 38 Nvidia trades between January and August 2026. The total transaction value was estimated at between $9.4 million and $28.3 million.
By August, the value of his Nvidia holdings was reported in a range of $13 million to $62 million.
The figures drew attention because the administration was making decisions that could affect Nvidia's business, particularly its access to China. The White House maintained that Trump's portfolio was independently managed.
But the most serious questions about Huang's relationship with the administration were about to emerge.
May 2026: Intelligence concerns and a last-minute China invitation
 Chinese President Xi Jinping stands alongside Jensen Huang, Founder, President and CEO of Nvidia during a welcoming ceremony for US President Donald Trump (not pictured) at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, China, May 14, 2026. File/Reuters
12 May 2026: According to reports by The Washington Post and ABC News, Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed Trump about intelligence concerns surrounding Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a business executive associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed.
US intelligence agencies reportedly suspected that Alice Huang had links to Chinese intelligence. These were allegations and intelligence assessments, not publicly established findings. Alice Huang is not related to Jensen Huang.
The briefing reportedly took place shortly before Huang joined Trump's delegation for a visit to China. Trump later said he had not known about the allegations at the time.
13 May 2026: Huang was initially left off the list of business leaders accompanying Trump to China.
That changed after Trump reportedly saw media coverage highlighting his absence and personally invited him to join the delegation.
Huang eventually boarded Air Force One during a refuelling stop in Alaska.
His inclusion was notable given the reported intelligence concerns. It also showed how closely the administration's China policy and Nvidia's commercial interests had become intertwined.
September and October 2026: Public recognition
 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his wife Lori Huang attend a state dinner hosted by US President Donald Trump for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in Washington, D.C., US, September 24, 2026. File/Reuters
24 September 2026: Huang and his wife, Lori, attended a White House state dinner hosted for Chinese President Xi Jinping.
His presence at the event was another indication of Nvidia's importance in the relationship between Washington and Beijing.
29 September 2026: Huang also attended a White House AI summit, where the administration discussed voluntary standards for the development and deployment of artificial intelligence.
8 October 2026: Trump presented Huang with the National Medal of Science at a White House event.
The award recognised Huang's contribution to science and technology. It came at a time when Nvidia's role in the AI industry had made its chief executive one of the most influential figures in global technology.
15 October 2026: The Washington Post reported that Nvidia and Apple had each committed $25 million towards Trump's planned White House ballroom project.
Nvidia said its contribution was being made to a nonpartisan trust and was unrelated to its business interests. Reuters said it could not independently verify the newspaper's report.
The reported contribution was separate from the silicon wafer Huang had presented to Trump in October 2025.
November 2026: Huang resigns, then returns
 Picture taken June 2, 2024. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang greets Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang after delivering his keynote speech at COMPUTEX 2024 in Taipei, Taiwan, June 2, 2024. File/Reuters
12 November 2026: Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive after reports emerged about extramarital relationships, including one involving Alice Huang. The allegations also raised questions about possible links to Chinese intelligence and the security implications for Nvidia.
The company said its board had accepted his resignation. Huang's departure sent shockwaves through the technology industry, given his central role in Nvidia's growth and the global AI boom.
Nvidia shares came under pressure following the news.
The company said it had no reason to believe that its secrets or national security had been compromised. It also began an investigation into whether foreign intelligence efforts had targeted Huang.
The allegations against Alice Huang were not proof that she was a Chinese intelligence operative.
Mid-November 2026
Trump repeatedly backed Huang's return, arguing that Nvidia needed its co-founder at the helm. Several prominent technology figures and investors also supported his reinstatement.
The Nvidia board initially appeared reluctant to reverse its decision. Its chairman had indicated that Huang would not be rehired because his conduct was inconsistent with the company's standards and code of conduct.
23 November 2026: Nvidia announced that it was reinstating Huang as chief executive with immediate effect. The board approved the decision unanimously.
The company said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's return did not pose a national security risk. It also said its investigation into possible foreign intelligence targeting would continue.
Trump took credit for the reversal. In an interview with CNBC, he said he had spoken to board members and convinced them to bring Huang back.
"I spoke to them. Let me put it this way: And I convinced them. I made the deal," Trump said.
Nvidia shares surged more than 30 per cent after the announcement, adding close to $1 trillion to the company's market value, according to Reuters.
The decision, however, did not end the scrutiny. US lawmakers from both parties questioned the board's move and called for tougher oversight of advanced chip exports to China. Huang is also expected to face questions from congressional committees.
A relationship shaped by business and geopolitics
The story of Trump and Huang is not simply one of two powerful men becoming closer. It is also a story of how the AI race has brought corporate interests, national security and US foreign policy into the same conversation.
For Trump, Nvidia is central to his ambition to keep the United States ahead in artificial intelligence. The company is also a major player in domestic manufacturing and international technology partnerships.
For Huang, access to Washington matters because US export rules can determine where Nvidia sells its most advanced chips. The company's ability to compete in China, expand in the Gulf and build manufacturing capacity in the US is closely tied to decisions made by the administration.
Their relationship has moved through awkward meetings, international trips, public praise, policy negotiations and a corporate crisis. Trump's intervention in Huang's reinstatement has taken that relationship into new territory.
But questions about Nvidia's China business, export-control compliance and the allegations surrounding Huang remain unresolved. The board's decision to bring him back may have restored the company's familiar leadership. It has not ended the political and national security debate around the world's leading AI chipmaker.

news.title: Democrats clinch historic House majority
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP):

House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

Democrats have so far gained 44 House seats from where they started on Election Day, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump’s first midterm in 2018

The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.

Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.

The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.

The Democrats’ majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt-era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.

It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.

“Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure,” said Democratic Representative Jason Crow of Colorado, a former Army Ranger.

“There are people dying in this country and people losing their healthcare, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorised from ICE,” he said earlier this month at the Capitol, referring to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. “If you don’t feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don’t belong under this Capitol dome.”

 Election rout creates a mandate to govern 

The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump.

Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.

The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans’ Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.

Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.

“This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen,” said progressive leader Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-NY, at the Capitol.

She called the big numbers “a mandate for change”.

Representative Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75 per cent of their time on affordability issues and 25 per cent on accountability.

“Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it’s affecting the people,” he said.

For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump’s financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: “How does that affect people’s pocketbooks?”

The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to “blatant criminality”.

 A new generation of leaders 

After House Speaker Mike Johnson, struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority — meaning a few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.

Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on January 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.

“We’re not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it’s okay,” said Rep. Troy Carter, who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They’re far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.

Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families,” Jordan said.

The GOP’s high-water marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

news.title: Asia Power Index: The G2.5 world is here, but India’s neighbourhood continues to trouble it
news.text:
Stare at the Lowy Institute's 2026 Asia Power Index chart for a while and the outline of the new world order starts to show itself. Two long bars sit at the top: the United States at 78.9 and China at 73.6. Some distance below them, in a tier of its own, is India at 40.5. Then the chart falls away sharply to a crowd of thirteen "middle powers", with Japan at their head on 38.6.
Last October, in an essay I called "The G2.5 World", I argued that China had not displaced America so much as joined it, and that India had become the third pivot of the system. My phrase was that India was a "half" that was really a full pole, wooed by both Washington and Beijing and beholden to neither. A year on, the most rigorous annual stocktake of power in the Indo-Pacific has drawn a picture that is very close to that one.
Start with the G2. My claim was that the United States had come to accept China's structural parity, less out of goodwill than necessity. The 2026 numbers back that up. When Lowy started the index in 2018, America led China by roughly ten points. The lead is now 5.3 points, the smallest in the index's history, and the gap in military capability has never been narrower.
How the gap closed matters as much as the fact that it did. China hardly moved this year, slipping a tenth of a point. Most of the narrowing came from America's own fall of 1.6 points. US diplomatic influence dropped six points to 76.7, its steepest fall on record and its fourth decline in a row. Lowy attributes this to the Iran war, punitive tariffs and loose talk of scaling back military exercises with South Korea. A superpower that can no longer outrun its rival eventually has to learn to share the road with it. When Donald Trump described his Busan meeting with Xi Jinping as a "G2" summit, he was saying so out loud. Lowy has now put numbers to it.
The second part of the argument, about India, is to my mind the more consequential one. India crossed Lowy's 40-point threshold for a "major power" in 2025. This year it did more than cling on: it gained half a point, and its gap with China, at around 33 points, is the narrowest it has been since 2018. Nobody should pretend 33 points is a small distance. What is new is that the gap is shrinking.
Look also at the arrows beside each country on the chart. Japan, South Korea, Indonesia and New Zealand, the Asian democracies America leans on most, are all pointing downwards. Japan was long assumed to be the region's natural second balancer. It has slipped from 38.8 to 38.6, and a revolving door of prime ministers in Tokyo has not helped. In the wide space between the two superpowers and everyone else, India is the only country going up the chart.
The fine print of India's score is even more revealing. Its diplomatic influence stands at 70.3, not far below a weakened United States, and regional experts rated Narendra Modi the second most effective leader in Asia, behind only Xi. Its biggest gain this year came in cultural influence, which rose by 2.3 points. Its defence networks rose 2.1 points, helped by BrahMos sales in Southeast Asia, so India is now arming the region as well as courting it. A swing state is not judged by tonnage alone. It is judged by how useful it can be to everyone without belonging to anyone. India sits in the Quad, the SCO and Brics all at once. In 2025, it took 50 per cent American tariffs without either giving in or drifting into Beijing's orbit. A strict G2 reading would have forced it to pick a side. It refused, and its standing rose anyway.
The uncomfortable numbers deserve the same attention. India's economic capability fell 0.7 points this year, its sharpest drop, to a modest 26.4. This is the old "power gap" Lowy has pointed to since 2018, where India's influence keeps running ahead of its industrial base. Its lead over Japan is under two points. Hunter Marston, who leads the index at Lowy, still describes the regional balance as "markedly bipolar".
None of that undercuts the G2.5 reading. It is precisely why the figure is two and a half and not three. I never claimed India was a third superpower. My point was that the system is neither bipolar nor fully multipolar, but a balance held in place by the constraints each power places on the others. At the very top, Asia is bipolar. Who tips the balance is a different question, and there the answer is increasingly India.
What does all this mean for the wider order? Four things stand out to me.
The first is that any G2 condominium now comes with a built-in brake. Washington and Beijing could quietly divide Asia into spheres only if nobody outside the pair had the heft to object. India's solitary place in the major-power tier is that objection. Whatever deals the two strike, on rare earths, chips or tariffs, now has to account for a country of 1.4 billion whose diplomatic standing is not far off America's.
The second is that the much-discussed "middle power moment" has a ceiling, and Lowy's own 2026 launch acknowledged the limits of middle-power agency. With Japan, South Korea and Indonesia all sliding, coalitions of middle powers cannot hold off the G2 alone. They need an anchor, and the only one that is rising is India. More and more of their strategies quietly assume it.
The third is that the "half" has to become whole in economic terms. A pole resting on diplomacy and culture is real, but it is brittle. India's diplomatic score is almost three times its economic capability score, and that imbalance is its single biggest strategic weakness. What will carry India from 40.5 towards 50 is factories, exports and homegrown technology, not more summits.
The fourth concerns the neighbourhood, which is becoming harder to manage. Pakistan now sits on the middle-power line at 15 points, with its arrow pointing up. North Korea, rising just below it, has consequences that reach well beyond the Korean peninsula. A swing state keeps its freedom to swing only as long as its borders are quiet and its region reasonably stable. A Pakistan that feels stronger, and whose friends in Beijing are enjoying near-parity with Washington, is not a recipe for quiet.
An index cannot measure civilisational confidence or strategic patience. What it can show is where the weight is shifting. In 2026, it shows two superpowers drawing closer and one rising power standing on its own between them. That is the G2.5 world, and the evidence for it is now hard to dismiss.
(Hindol Sengupta is professor of international relations at O. P. Jindal Global University and author of the forthcoming ‘The Second Republic: India as a Civilizational State’, Bloomsbury, 2027. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

news.title: Trumps feared Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could move to chine, lobbied for his return
news.text:
New York: US President Donald Trump, who lobbied to get Jensen Huang his job back as Nvidia CEO, feared the company’s founder could have gone to China.

“I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, ‘Hey, how would you like to come to China’,” Trump said on Monday (local time) after the Nvidia board reinstated him.

“If Jensen was angry enough, if he was treated badly, maybe he could do that,” Trump told CNBC.

He added, “Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you they would give him whatever he wanted.”

Huang built Nvidia from a maker of chips for gaming computers into the tech behemoth whose advanced chips power most of the major Western artificial intelligence (AI) companies.

As Trump has acknowledged, the US lead in AI may hinge on Nvidia’s performance.

Trump said he spoke to Nvidia’s board “and I convinced them” to bring him back 11 days after he had resigned in disgrace after admitting to an affair with a women suspected of links to China’s intelligence agencies.

He noted the Taiwan-born entrepreneur has “got a little (Chinese) blood in him”.

The Beijing government claims the independent democratic country, Taiwan, as its territory.

Trump returned last week from a visit to China during which he met China’s President Xi Jinping.

He said at a news conference on Friday, “I did discuss that (Nvidia and Huang) with President Xi, and he said, ‘Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He’s a brilliant man’.”

Trump celebrated Huang’s return by posting on Truth Social an altered risque version of the iconic picture of him after he narrowly missed an assassination attempt during the 2025 presidential campaign.

He replaced his image of him waving his fist in the air in triumph in that picture with Huang holding up a red bra and Nvidia’s logo swapped for the US flag in the background.

That seemed to ridicule the furore over Huang’s affairs with Alice Huang (no relation), allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset, and a woman working at Nvidia.

Trump, a veteran of three marriages and several affairs, posted under the picture, “Congratulations to NVIDIA on having made, what I consider to be, an absolutely GREAT decision!”

Alice Huang, with whom the Nvidia CEO admitted to having an affair, was an executive with Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company with links to China, that has allegedly diverted advanced Nvidia chips to China.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also the National Security Adviser, had reportedly warned Trump about Alice Huang’s alleged China intelligence links.

The Commerce Department on Monday blacklisted Megaspeed, barring it from receiving advanced Nvidia chips, amid reports that the Justice Department was investigating allegations that it diverted chips to China.

Trump said the US government had “exonerated” Huang of having done anything wrong.

However, the Republican-controlled Congress is not convinced and is gearing up to delve further into the Huang and Nvidia issues before the Democrats take over in January.

“Congress has much to investigate, and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other,” Tom Cotton, the Republican chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said on X.

It “is just the tip of the iceberg”, he said.

Brian Mast, the Republican chairman of the House of Representatives Foreign Relations Committee, called the allegations “extremely concerning”.

Huang is due to face an interview next Tuesday with the Foreign Affairs Committee, which is investigating Huang and Nvidia jointly with the select committees on intelligence and China.

That will be followed by a public hearing the next day with the Senate Banking Committee.

Next year, when the Democrats take over Congress following their spectacular victory in the midterm elections, Huang has company, and Trump administration officials will face even more gruelling probes.

“Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other Nvidia executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” Chuck Schumer, the Democratic Party leader in the Senate, said on X.

Schumer, likely to become the majority leader in the Senate next year, said, “Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasising that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat.”

Hakeem Jeffries, who will be the speaker of the House, warned that there will be “a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by Nvidia and corrupt abuse of power by (Commerce Secretary) Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce”.

news.title: Trump Just Handed His Opponents The Mother Of All Presidential Scandals
news.text:
For all of President Donald Trump’s fake talk about the working class and nationalism over the past 10 years, his second term has been defined by a series of power grabs on behalf of securing the fortunes of an oligarchic overclass and their future as the supreme rulers of society.

This project has led to a glut of self-enrichment by government officials, seemingly corrupt deals to aid corporate titans and the use of executive power to enable corporate and governmental lawlessness.

Now, after Democrats won a generational election victory in November running against the White House’s top-down class war and the resulting decline in affordability and quality of life, Trump has handed the incoming Congress the mother of all scandal.

It features Watergate’s abuse of executive power, the Iran-Contra Affair’s undermining of national security, Monicagate’s salacious details and Enron’s corporate malfeasance, all wrapped in the too-big-to-fail dynamics that fuelled the global financial crisis, with a side of AI and data centre anxiety to boot.

It’s such an obvious scandal narrative for Democrats looking to marry their priorities of delivering on affordability while performing oversight of the Trump administration and corporate bad actors that you’d think it was written by one of the AI chatbots that Nvidia’s chips help power.

To recap, Huang, perhaps the most important CEO involved in the largest industrial buildout in generations, had an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who US intelligence determined is a likely Chinese intelligence asset engaged in smuggling high-tech chips into mainland China.

Nvidia sold those chips to her Singaporean company, Megaspeed, and those were then moved into China in violation of US export controls.

Next, Trump was informed about all of this, first in October 2025 and then again in May 2026, and did nothing.

The Commerce Department under Secretary Howard Lutnick, tasked with enforcing export control laws, not only did nothing but approved Nvidia sales to Megaspeed despite ongoing investigations into chip smuggling.

Finally, when Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang was revealed, the Nvidia board removed him as CEO, citing national security concerns. Alice Huang was sanctioned by Singapore and has since disappeared back in China.

Then, as AI stocks, which now account for more than 50% of US stock market gains, tumbled and the AI boom, questionably financed by Nvidia acting as a kind of central bank, began to teeter, Trump stepped in to personally force Nvidia to reinstate Huang as CEO.

Here we have the most important CEO of the most important company in the world engaged in an affair with an alleged foreign government asset he possibly conspired with to violate laws meant to protect US national security — all to prop up the AI chip market and juice the stock market while the president knew about it and looked the other way. And that doesn’t even begin to tell the whole story.

The Huang affair is like a turducken for Trump’s second-term controversies. Cut through the top layer of sex and spies, and you’ll find the White House ballroom, the president’s crypto company, donations to inaugural funds and presidential libraries, stock trades and the self-enrichment of the president and his billionaire Cabinet.

Huang and Nvidia contributed $25 million to the White House ballroom that is Trump’s obsession. Huang attended a $1 million-per-donor dinner at Mar-a-Lago to fund Trump’s lavish inauguration. Huang pushed for Trump to authorise chip sales to the United Arab Emirates, which Trump did after a top UAE official invested $500 million in his crypto company.

And, of course, Trump purchased tens of millions in Nvidia stock in 2025 and even sold $1 million worth after being told Huang was potentially having an affair.

Did these donations and investments corrupt Trump’s decision-making process when he let Huang off the hook?

Beyond Trump, there’s Lutnick, who oversees the enforcement of the export controls Huang may have violated. 

Cantor Fitzgerald, Lutnick’s firm that is now run by his sons, held more than $1 billion in Nvidia stock in 2025. The firm claims that these positions “arise from equity swaps executed for clients.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and members of Congress accused Lutnick of refusing to investigate and enforce the export control laws on Nvidia and the company headed by Alice Huang, Megaspeed. A Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed was spiked after Nvidia’s intervention, The New York Times reported.

Lutnick previously wriggled his way out of trouble by contributing $25 million to Trump’s presidential library fund as the president weighed firing him after documents revealed in 2025 that he had visited the private island of deceased sex criminal Jeffrey Epstein. “Trump stopped talking about replacing Lutnick” after that contribution, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Upon word that Huang had been reinstated, Cantor Fitzgerald released a statement headlined: “All is right in the world again.” The Commerce Department belatedly added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist on Monday afternoon.

There are so many questions to unravel in the Huang affair. Questions of not just “Who knew what when?” but also “Who made how much when?”

Huang’s reinstatement on Trump’s orders also raises questions about Trump’s expansion of executive power in telling Nvidia’s board that Huang was absolved of all wrongdoing.

“Did you give the board of directors an assurance that Jensen Huang would not be prosecuted at all for anything?” CNBC’s Eamon Javers asked Trump on Monday.

“I didn’t use the word ‘prosecuted,’ but I said that we believe … he’s absolutely fine. I gave them enough assurance,” Trump responded.

What is important to remember here, amid all the official assurances that Huang is in the clear, is that Trump has asserted a total right to interfere and direct actions at every agency within the executive branch. This is a right the Supreme Court handed him in both the Trump v. US decision that granted him immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts and the Trump v. Slaughter decision that ended the independence of certain agencies.

For this reason, there is no real assurance that Jensen Huang did not commit any crimes or that Alice Huang is not a Chinese intelligence asset. There is, however, an assurance that the Trump administration will allow them to get away with it by not investigating or enforcing the law.

What the Huang affair shows is that Trump has adopted his Access Hollywood maxim that “when you’re a star, they just let you do it,” and turned it into the ethos of not only the government, but the economy and society writ large.

Unravelling what happened here will be necessary to stop the moral rot from permanently taking root.
