news.title: Myth of the founder endures as Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia
news.text:
Jensen Huang has been reinstated as chief executive of Nvidia, 11 days after stepping down. 

Blink and you might have missed it. The leather jacket-clad Nvidia founder had left the tech giant following revelations about his extramarital affairs, including one with a client whom US intelligence suspects is a Chinese spy.

His departure plunged the company into crisis and sent its stock downwards. 

We have been here before. OpenAI’s board ousted its cofounder and chief executive Sam Altman in November 2023, claiming it no longer had confidence in his ability to continue leading the company. 

It took only five days to bring Altman back, after the board came under pressure from Microsoft, a key backer. The tech giant offered Altman, cofounder Greg Brockman, who had resigned in support of him, and any other departing OpenAI staff jobs at the tech giant. More than 700 staff also threatened to resign if Altman was not brought back. 

Perhaps Nvidia staff were taking a leaf from OpenAI’s book when they started the “Stand With Jensen” petition, demanding that he be reinstated. At the last count, more than 200,000 people had signed it, including 10,000 Nvidia staff, almost 2,000 former employees and 108,000 who claimed to be shareholders. All of that was self-reported, however, and not verified by the petition’s creators. Among the big names in tech who appeared on the letter were Y Combinator founder Garry Tan, Uber’s Travis Kalanick, Tesla chief executive Elon Musk, and YouTube cofounder Steve Chen. 

[ Nvidia shares jump over 30% on reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executiveOpens in new window ]

As recently as a week ago, Nvidia’s board had dismissed the possibility of Huang returning. But it seems that the company came under pressure from the Trump administration. The Nvidia founder’s return did not, in the White House’s opinion, present a national security risk. And according to US president Donald Trump, he convinced them to rehire Huang. 

That led to a bounce in both Nvidia’s stock, which added 30 per cent following the news, and the wider AI sector. 

It seems the myth of the founder, even one who makes questionable decisions, is alive and well.

I started to tell her about Scott and how he had really discovered the Nixon Tapes because he found Alexander Butterfield. Not letting me off the hook, Kagan asked again, "How did you do it?" Well, we interviewed five sitting justices and 170 law clerks. We got documentation. That's extraordinary, Kagan said. How did you get the documents? The justices must have approved the clerks giving you the documents? I shook my head. Not that we were aware. You make clerks now sign nondisclosure agreements, I noted. "Yes," she said.

I told her that Brennan and Marshall, the liberal justices on the court, would not help us. Well, who did? Rehnquist and White, I said. Kagan seemed surprised. I recounted the story of calling Justice Lewis Powell at the court one morning and him agreeing to meet. I said when and he said now. "I was in my pajamas, but told him I'd be there in half an hour." You must be fast, Kagan said. I was then, I joked. I was 79 now and slow.

Is all of this known about The Brethren? Kagan asked. I didn't have an answer so instead I dived into Blackmun's role in Roe v. Wade and how he had drafted the opinion at the Mayo Clinic library. "I thought the leak of the Dobbs decision was a public service," I told her, referencing the decision that had overturned Roe the previous year. I can't say I agree with that, Kagan said. Why do you think it's a public service? Well, the court took away a right that had been there for 50 years. The public needed to know so there could be a debate. Kagan didn't say anything.

I said from reporting more than 50 years on 10 presidents, I thought there was such a concentration of power in the presidency. Too much power.

She nodded. It's why Trump was able to get away with so much, I said. Kagan did not respond. Then I said, there's too much power in the Supreme Court maybe. She noticeably reacted to that, her head held a little higher, her posture stiffening. Her only reply was, "That's interesting."

"Are you happy on the court?" I asked her. No, I'm not, given the situation, Kagan replied. I was surprised at her candor.

As we parted ways, she smiled warmly and said she respected my work and I said I respected hers. Late that night I recorded a detailed voice memo of my conversation with Kagan for my assistant to transcribe. It is hard to tell who was interviewing who.

On Saturday, October 21, 2023, Elsa and I attended a dinner for the 50th anniversary of the Saturday Night Massacre hosted by the former Watergate special prosecutors at the WilmerHale law firm in downtown Washington. The main speaker was retired Supreme Court justice Stephen Breyer, who had been a junior Watergate prosecutor. Elsa sat next to Breyer at the dinner before switching seats with me. He had served 28 years on the Supreme Court and told her he was "forced out" so someone younger could take his place.

Later Gray told me it took five years for Clarence Thomas to recover. Justice Thomas's wife, Ginni Thomas, a conservative activist, approached me at a conference in Washington one day. She said after the hearings her husband was never really a whole person again. He hardened. Many conservatives, including attorney general for George H. W. Bush and for Donald Trump, Bill Barr, have said the hearings pushed Thomas to the hard right.
news.summary: Kagan sheds some light on her view about leaks, Dobbs, and the Court.
news.author: Josh Blackman,Tosin Akintola

news.title: How Chinese spies are using LinkedIn to obtain information from US officials
news.text:
“We spy on China; they spy on us. I think we spy better than they do,” said Donald Trump last week during a live interview with Fox News from Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Apec Summit.
However, latest reports suggest otherwise; Beijing’s espionage activities are becoming more advanced and much more extensive than what US authorities investigated earlier.
In fact, according to a CNN investigation, Chinese spies may be using fake job offers to get information from current and former US government employees. They are reportedly setting up fake consulting companies and posting job openings on platforms such as LinkedIn to approach people who may have access to sensitive government information.
Here's what we know so far.
Inside China’s spy racket using job offers
Instead of using cloak and dagger methods to gain information from the US, China has pivoted to using everyday websites such as LinkedIn to target their potential victims.
According to a CNN investigation, the Chinese followed a single pattern to target former and current American government officials. They made use of artificial intelligence and stolen identities to build professional-looking corporate websites before advertising well-paid consulting assignments on platforms such as LinkedIn.
In most cases, the job postings are vague and focus on China-related issues. They seek people with experience in areas such as international affairs, national security, military operations, and intelligence.
 Chinese spies are using sites such as LinkedIn to reach out to their potential targets in the US. Representational image/Reuters
The investigation further reveals that applicants are then asked to prepare research reports for the companies, and quite often, the person is not told who the actual client is. According to officials who spoke to CNN, the aim isn’t to obtain classified documents from a single individual. Instead, the Chinese are collecting smaller pieces of information from a large number of people and combining them to build a broader understanding of US policies, intelligence programmes and potential vulnerabilities.
As Holden Triplett, a former director of counterintelligence at the National Security Council during the first Trump administration, told CNN, “Even if everyone (the suspected Chinese operatives) are talking to is extremely careful and not revealing anything classified, they are talking to so many people (that) they might be able to get a view of (an intelligence) programme in totality,” Triplett said.
Forget James Bond, dead drops, and trillion-dollar AI superweapons.
The biggest Chinese intelligence dragnet of 2026 literally consisted of AI-generated recruiter headshots posting Canva “WE ARE HIRING! Defense Analyst” flyers on LinkedIn to phish laid-off clearance holders for remote freelance reports.
Look at the posters in that screenshot. They look like a 2019 Fiverr template for an affiliate marketing webinar, yet the FBI had to seize entire domains because former officials were actually taking the bait.
We spend all day arguing over frontier compute and cinematic honeytraps while national security secrets are getting exfiltrated through “Work From Home! Earn Money Online!” job boards. Get the fuck outta here !!!
— Daebak 앤디 (@MyDaebakCafe) November 23, 2026
When China tried to recruit former Pentagon official
Wes Bryant, who worked in a Pentagon office focused on minimising civilian harm in military operations, was among the many who reported that Chinese spies tried to recruit.
He told CNN that in January 2025 he received an email from a representative for a Malaysian think tank called MRDA. The mail to Bryant read, “I was truly impressed by your background and extensive experience in the military area. We are keen on collaborating with leading experts to help strengthen security efforts in Malaysia and the broader region.”
Taking up the offer after two months, Bryant wrote a staid report on how the Trump administration might approach a security pact with Australia and the UK, only using publicly available information.
Lily, the ‘representative’ from the Malaysian firm, then paid Bryant $1,200 (Rs 1.1 lakh). However, she came back to Bryant, saying the unnamed client thought there was “room for improvement.” Bryant believed this was a way to extract more information out of him.
Later, an analysis of MRDA showed that it used a Chinese-language font, and photos posted by one of the organisation’s representatives bore watermarks from RedNote, a popular Chinese social media platform.
Trump’s layoffs provide China with the perfect opportunity
According to the investigation, US President Donald Trump mass government layoffs helped the Chinese in their espionage activities.
Hundreds of thousands of workers were forced out of their jobs as Trump returned to the White House. This led to a large supply of unemployed people who possibly held valuable information.
Seeing this as an opportunity, China ramped up its efforts to recruit targets via job postings on websites. A former senior US intelligence official told CNN, “We created a vulnerability that was not necessary. We created access and opportunity to tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of people without the tools needed to deal with the Communist Party of China.”
 This isnt the first time that China's spies are using job portals to seek out targets. Representational image/AI generated
Job postings – an old Chinese spy playbook
Many experts note that this isn’t the first time that China has used job listing websites as part of its espionage activities.
Earlier in October, an ABC News report revealed that two suspected Chinese spies posed as employees of a think tank and targeted more than 100 individuals linked to Australia, including former Queensland premier and now Opposition Leader Steven Miles, an Australian Federal Police commander and several senior federal government officials.
In June, Washington and its Five Eyes intelligence partners, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the United Kingdom, also issued a warning about information obtained through fake consultancy schemes. In a report, the Five Eyes wrote that China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS) approached tens of thousands of US and Nato government staffers, military personnel, academics, and others with access to sensitive information through LinkedIn and other professional networking sites over recent years.
UK’s spy agency, MI5, also warned that Chinese spies are targeting UK government and military staff on job websites, including LinkedIn, to try to get access to classified or sensitive information.
In 2018, a Singaporean named Dickson Yeo set up a fake company and posted job ads to approach people in the US. Later, Yeo pleaded guilty to acting as an agent of Chinese intelligence. He was sentenced to 14 months in prison.
China’s response
Reacting to the investigation, a spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington said: “I am not familiar with what you mentioned. China opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called ‘Chinese spy’ narrative.”

news.title: Not Just a CEO Rescue: Trump's Bigger Game in Bringing Huang Back Decoded | Firstpost Live
news.text: Donald Trump and JD Vance played key roles in bringing Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO, less than two weeks after his resignation amid allegations surrounding an alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Behind the scenes, Trump personally contacted Nvidia's board, while Vance helped secure assurances over national security concerns. Huang's return was welcomed by cheering employees and triggered a massive market rally, adding more than $900 billion to Nvidia's market value. But the comeback has sparked political backlash, with lawmakers demanding answers over the White House intervention and alleged links to Chinese intelligence. Griha Atul tells you more on Firstpost Live.

news.title: Inside the ‘war room’ that lobbied Donald Trump to bring back Nvidia’s Jensen Huang
news.text:
Over the course of the weekend, Trump and Vance’s engagement focused on convincing the board that Huang’s affair with Alice Huang did not mean he was exposed as a potential national security risk.

Treasury secretary Scott Bessent went out on Sunday to soften his earlier stance, having a week before accused the company of artificially inflating its revenue through illicit China sales and called for a wholesale leadership shake-up.

Those involved in the campaign viewed Bessent’s reversal as evidence they were making progress. Trump’s intervention with the board proved decisive.

On Monday, after Huang was returned to his post, Baker posted on X: "This is why America is the greatest country on earth. Every part of Jensen’s story would have only been possible in America."

Inside Nvidia, employees responded to Huang’s return with a mixture of elation and surprise. Even those who had quietly hoped for Huang’s reappointment told the FT they had not expected it to happen so quickly.

One longtime employee said that staff who had known Jensen for years were shocked at the context of his downfall, in particular the surge in press reports about his well-known brutal management style.

"He has always behaved like this. People of a certain generation are thinking: why now?" said one.

Despite running Nvidia for 33 years and owning 3.5 per cent of the company, Huang does not have the supervoting shares that enable other founder-CEOs, such as Mark Zuckerberg, to overrule their boards.

"If I’m Jensen Huang, my first question today is, 'How can I get me some of those super voting shares so I can tell everybody to f*** off next time'," said one person who had worked with Huang in Washington.

Huang’s return does not signal an end to the company’s troubles. Trump on Monday said the US attorney general’s office had "done a very thorough investigation" into Huang’s conduct and "exonerated" him. But both Democratic and Republican lawmakers on Monday were outraged.

Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter have been summoned to congressional hearings next week.

No member of the cabinet outside Vance had publicly endorsed Huang’s return on Monday. Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, himself under scrutiny over Nvidia’s ability to sell to Megaspeed on his watch, was not involved in the board discussions, according to one person close to him.

Internally, Huang’s personal management style, exercising close control over subordinates aided by his daughter and son-in-law, with no formal succession planning, has led to scrutiny about governance.

One longtime associate of board chair Jones said the decision to reinstate Huang would do little to assuage public concern and market worries around AI.

"The midterm elections showed that the wider public is deeply sceptical about all things AI," the person said. "The Jensen affair masks a growing market consensus that the debt-leveraged speculative data centre build-out is quite fragile."

It also does nothing to reduce scrutiny of Nvidia’s board, which is stacked with longtime Huang allies and lacks any major tech or national security figures.

"While we are happy to have Jensen back, the on-again, off-again response from the board is, frankly, clown-like," Bernstein analysts wrote on Monday, adding that it "brings up legitimate questions as to their judgment and process, which has to make one wonder how they come to their other important decisions".

Others were more blunt. “Corporate governance has gone the way of the dodo,” said one large Nvidia investor.

news.title: Trump Claims He Helped Bring Jensen Huang Back To Nvidia, Feared China Could Hire Him
news.text: Donald Trump has revealed that he feared China would try to bring Jensen Huang on board to lead Huawei or another major Chinese tech company if Nvidia did not reinstate him as CEO. Nvidia board chairman Harvey C. Jones said the board unanimously backed Huang's return after discussions with him.After returning, Huang, 63, said he was “honored to return to NVIDIA” and lead the company at the beginning of a new industrial revolution. We have to protect our geniuses, and he's certainly a genius,” Trump was cited as saying by Reuters. ALSO READ: Jensen Huang Is Back: Nvidia Reinstates Ousted CEO 11 Days After His Shock ExitTrump said Xi respected Huang more than almost anyone else and believed China could try to hire him if he felt he was being treated unfairly in the US. “I will tell you that his respect for Jensen is so great, and I mean it was just, you know, he viewed him on a different level than just about anybody,” Trump said.“You know, this guy could end up paying him a fortune to let him run a company in China,” he added. Trump also said Huang could become unhappy with his treatment in the US and consider moving to China.“Jensen could be angry at our country, you know, and say, ‘I'm going to go to China.' Well, he's got the Blackwell in his brain. It's his baby. That's the thing. He's got a little blood in him, you know. He's got a little blood there. ‘How would you like to come to China and head up Huawei, and head up one of our companies?'” Trump stated.He also argued that losing Huang's technical knowledge would be a bigger concern for the US than the national security allegations surrounding him. The controversy surrounding Huang followed after reports of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. US officials have alleged that Alice Huang was working with Chinese intelligence. news.title: Senior Republican senator backs Board of Peace: ‘Israel must fulfill its commitments’
news.text: U.S. criticism of Israel's handling of the Gaza Strip is reaching some of its supporters on Capitol Hill, with Republican Sen. Dave McCormick calling on Israel to fulfill its commitments under President Donald Trump's peace plan. McCormick, who chairs the Senate Foreign Relations Committee's Middle East subcommittee, was responding to a Ynet report revealing growing frustration within the Board of Peace over Israel's conduct in Gaza. Writing on X, McCormick said he agreed with Trump and the Board of Peace that immediate action was needed. "Hamas must disarm, and Israel must fulfill its commitments. Failure to act risks squandering a historic opportunity and international buy-in," he wrote. The senator shared Ynet's interview with Josh Gruenbaum, a senior adviser to the Board of Peace, who warned that if Israel continued to delay implementation of the plan, the board could hand responsibility for Gaza back to the United Nations. Gruenbaum argued that Israel was preventing the board from testing whether Hamas genuinely intended to honor its commitment to disarm. "We feel like we're in a holding pattern. Hamas verbally agreed to move forward. They verbally agreed to disarm. And we're at a standstill because of political elements within Netanyahu's government that have not allowed us to move forward and test whether Hamas will keep its word," he said. "If we put that to the test and discover that Hamas is not honoring its commitment, we will publicly speak out against it and act accordingly. But that test must be allowed to take place." Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and adviser, also warned Monday that Israel risked becoming an international pariah if it continued on its current trajectory. Kushner said Israel was at a crossroads, with an opportunity to emerge from the tragedy of October 7 more secure and better integrated into the world, or continue on a path toward "global-pariah status." Kushner, one of the architects of Trump's 20-point plan for Gaza, also revealed that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had doubted whether U.S. efforts to end the war and secure the release of the hostages would succeed. "Bibi didn't think we could do it," he said. According to Kushner, he had spent recent months trying to persuade Netanyahu to allow Gaza's reconstruction plan to advance, but the prime minister's refusal had left the process stalled. Board of Peace representatives returned to Israel last week with a brief presentation outlining the severity and urgency of the situation in Gaza. Their message was clear: The Israeli government was running out of time to implement the plan. The board argued that while Hamas had accepted Trump's 20-point plan, Israel had "refused to provide reciprocal commitments," warning that the longer the situation continued, the higher the costs would be. The presentation's final slide, titled "Other alternatives for Gaza," outlined possible scenarios in which Trump's Board of Peace would no longer oversee the territory's future. These included a future U.S. administration and Congress pursuing a different reconstruction plan, or the United Nations Security Council taking responsibility, potentially through the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA). Other possibilities listed were the Palestinian Authority and, finally, Hamas itself. It was not the first time the board had publicly criticized Israel. About two weeks ago, days after former British Prime Minister Tony Blair visited Israel and met with President Isaac Herzog, the board issued a sharply worded statement following flooding in Gaza, calling on Israel to immediately approve the entry of winter preparedness supplies. The statement accused Israel of exacerbating Gaza's humanitarian crisis by delaying approval for essential equipment. Its demand that Hamas lay down its weapons and transfer governing authority to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza received only passing mention. The statement followed heavy rains that flooded tent encampments across Gaza. The board said it had been pressing Israel for months to authorize the entry of essential materials and equipment in accordance with its commitments under the Sharm el-Sheikh agreement. Israel, for its part, rejected the criticism. The Prime Minister's Office said Israel had assisted with winter preparedness efforts in coordination with the Board of Peace, the UN, international organizations and donor countries, placing full responsibility for the situation on Hamas. "To date, Hamas has not handed over a single weapon and continues to hold Gaza's residents hostage to its rule of terror," the office said. The Prime Minister's Office stressed that Israel was working closely with the United States and the Board of Peace and remained committed to the success of President Trump's 20-point plan. Under the plan, Hamas must disarm and the Gaza Strip must be demilitarized before reconstruction can begin.
news.summary: Sen. Dave McCormick responds to Ynet’s report on mounting frustration over stalled Gaza reconstruction, warning that a historic opportunity could be lost; his remarks follow Jared Kushner’s warning that Israel risks becoming an international pariah

news.title: US flew drone over Mexican territory to help capture drug lord in Sinaloa
news.text: MEXICO CITY: The United States flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to help the government track down and capture a top drug lord over the weekend in Sinaloa, Mexican security officials said Monday.The recent detention of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro” illustrates increasing law enforcement cooperation between the neighboring countries, but U.S. involvement in Mexican security operations has long been a touchy subject.U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to crack down on cartels, while Mexico has repeatedly underscored its sovereignty. On Monday, Sheinbaum emphasized that U.S. forces were not allowed to operate on the ground in Mexico and the governments were only sharing intelligence.“This case in particular demonstrates the capacity of the armed forces” of Mexico to make major detentions, Sheinbaum said.The U.S. has sought to line up allies across Latin America to allow U.S. forces to operate in their territories, with mixed responses from across the region.The weekend detention of the capo, who was one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives, triggered a burst of violence in the northern state of Sinaloa that left 20 people dead in the city of Guasave. Among them were four soldiers and 16 suspected criminals, Mexican officials said Monday.Defense Secretary Gen. Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said Monday that the capture of Meza Flores and 16 members of his criminal group was the result of “very important intelligence sharing” with U.S. authorities over the past three months to pinpoint Meza Flores’ location in Guasave.In the week leading up to Meza Flores’ capture, that included authorizing the U.S. to fly intelligence drones over Mexican territory to assist Mexican law enforcement to later surround the capo and go in for the capture, Trevilla Trejo and other Mexican officials said. They emphasized that the intelligence mission was carried out in compliance with Mexican law..On Monday, Mexico's prosecutors' office announced that it had formally charged Meza Flores and two other alleged cartel members with illegal possession of firearms and possession of methamphetamine with the intent to sell, adding that the three were flown to Mexico City over the weekend following their capture.Authorities also highlighted that the U.S. has an existing extradition request for Meza Flores for drug trafficking charges, leaving open the possibility that the cartel boss may be sent north to face justice.His capture was celebrated by Mexican and U.S. law enforcement as a major blow to criminal groups in the region.The U.S. government highlighted its intelligence support in the operation, but did not immediately provide more details about the use of the surveillance drone when asked on Monday.Meza Flores led the Beltran Leyva organization and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. He was also a key ally of a Sinaloa Cartel faction known as “Los Mayos," which is locked in a brutal territorial war against another cartel faction in the Mexican state.The capture of Meza Flores was the latest in a string of targeted operations against cartel kingpins by Mexican authorities, the largest of which was the February killing of Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as " El Mencho."While the captures show that the government is doubling down on its fight against crime, many experts were quick to emphasize that the strategy could backfire.In previous anti-crime offensives in Mexico and other parts of Latin America, knocking out cartel leaders without debilitating the entire criminal structure around them has largely only fueled bloody power struggles between cartel factions. That has been the case in recent years in Sinaloa..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Dollar climbs as renewed AI euphoria fuels Fed hike bets
news.text: SINGAPORE: The dollar ‌hovered near a 20-month ​high on Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia's CEO breathed new life into the AI rally and stoked expectations that the recovery would give the Federal Reserve greater scope to raise rates further. Against the resurgent greenback, the euro languished near an over 18-month low at $1.0907 after sliding 0.6% overnight, while sterling similarly struggled to bounce from a one-year low and last bought $1.3037. The dollar firmed at 104.32 against a ⁠basket of currencies , having peaked at 104.53 in the previous session. Nvidia on Monday reinstated Huang as CEO under pressure from US President Donald Trump, a stunning reversal following his resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged spy for China. The move reignited the AI euphoria and sparked a blistering rally ‌across equities, with Nvidia adding roughly $950 billion to its market capitalisation overnight. "It's really hard to say what Jensen Huang's comeback as the CEO of Nvidia means to the whole AI investment boom, but judging by the equity market ‌movement, investors seem pretty excited about his reinstatement and markets are buying into ‌the whole AI narrative again," said Carol Kong, a currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. "For now, it ‌seems to be a positive for the ‌AI narrative that has been a crucial pillar of the US exceptionalism story that has supported the US dollar." Traders have now fully priced in a ​25-basis-point Fed hike next month ‌and see a slim chance of ​an outsized 50bp move, up from zero a ⁠day earlier, according to the CME FedWatch tool. The equity market rout over the past week, led by a heavy selloff in technology and chip stocks, had prompted investors to pare back bets on further Fed hikes due ​to uncertainty over how much ⁠more tightening the economy ⁠could withstand. "Our US economists have been flagging that tighter financial conditions and lower equity valuations could limit the Fed's appetite for further tightening, though (Monday's) move is reversing some of that pressure," said Citi markets analyst Preston Pagli. The yen eased ⁠slightly to 159.06 per dollar in the early Asian session, while the Aussie was pinned near an 11-month low at $0.6627. The New Zealand dollar similarly struggled at $0.5450, not far from Monday's 17-year trough of $0.5434. The Aussie has come under immense pressure in recent sessions on the back of a repricing of domestic rate expectations, with markets now fully pricing in a rate cut next August and a total of 50bp ‌worth of easing by the end of 2027. Analysts at J.P. Morgan said in a note that short positions in the Australian dollar against ​the greenback have "accummulated substantially", with bearish positioning reaching "extreme levels in some cases" by their metrics. "Looking first at options, AUD puts have been outnumbering calls for several months now. Early in this process, it seemed reasonable to assume that this might simply be macro hedging, rather than actual outright directional positioning. But the flows have ​probably migrated to the latter of ‌late," they said.

news.title: Foreign Investors Return To India. What's Driving Rs 1 Lakh Crore Inflows?
news.text: Stock Market Today: Foreign investors, who spent much of the past two years pulling money out of Indian equities, appear to be changing their stance. But this time, the reason may have less to do with India's growth story and more to do with growing concerns around the global artificial intelligence (AI) trade.Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) invested roughly Rs 1 lakh crore in Indian markets as of November 19, 2026. This marks a sharp reversal after months of heavy selling. Between January and October 2026 alone, foreign investors withdrew Rs 3.6 lakh crore, or around $38 billion, from Indian equities.According to Mitesh Dalal, Head of Broking at Sanctum Wealth, the latest inflows reflect a broader shift in global investment preferences. Investors are increasingly moving away from technology-heavy markets and looking at economies that could benefit from a possible unwinding of the AI trade.Why Are Foreign Investors Returning To India?Since September 2024, global investors have increasingly favoured technology and AI-driven markets such as the US, Taiwan and South Korea.India, with its consumption-led economy, was among the markets that faced the pressure of this shift in capital. However, the global investment narrative appears to be changing.The 2026 US midterm elections, in which Donald Trump's Republicans lost control of both houses of Congress, have added to concerns about the future of the AI trade.The Democratic victory has raised expectations of greater scrutiny of domestic AI infrastructure, data centres and semiconductor companies. This has fuelled concerns about tighter oversight of businesses that have benefited from the global AI boom.The resulting selloff in AI-linked stocks has encouraged investors to look beyond traditional technology-heavy markets.Dalal told NDTV that India has emerged as an attractive destination in this changing investment environment, particularly as investors reassess their exposure to the AI trade.Cooling Crude Oil Prices Add To India's AppealAnother factor supporting foreign investor sentiment is the moderation in crude oil prices. Brent crude, which had climbed above $100 per barrel, has cooled to around $93 per barrel as concerns over supply disruptions have eased.This is particularly important for India, which imports a large share of its crude oil requirements. Lower oil prices can ease pressure on the country's import bill, inflation and current account deficit. They can also provide some relief to the rupee and corporate margins.For foreign investors, this improves India's relative attractiveness at a time when global markets are reassessing their exposure to expensive AI-linked stocks.Have Indian Stock Market Valuations Become Attractive?Valuations have also played an important role in bringing foreign investors back. The sharp correction in Indian equities has brought the valuations of the Nifty 50 and other benchmark indices closer to levels seen around the Covid-era market troughs.This has made Indian equities more attractive from a relative valuation perspective. According to Dalal, India has emerged as one of the strongest beneficiaries of the anti-AI trade. This is particularly relevant as other emerging markets, including Brazil and Indonesia, continue to face macroeconomic challenges.For foreign investors looking to diversify away from technology-heavy markets, India's consumption-driven economy and relatively attractive valuations offer an alternative.Is This The Beginning Of A Structural FPI Comeback?Despite the recent inflows, investors may want to avoid interpreting the reversal as the beginning of a sustained foreign investment cycle. Several risks could still change the direction of global capital flows.Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East remain a concern. Any escalation could push crude oil prices higher and hurt sentiment towards oil-importing economies such as India.There is also the possibility of the global AI trade gaining momentum again. If investors return to technology stocks, money could once again move away from markets such as India.Domestic challenges could add to the uncertainty. An El Nino-driven rise in food inflation could affect household budgets and consumption demand. Persistent weakness in rural demand could also weigh on corporate earnings.Dalal cautions that the recent FPI inflows should not automatically be seen as evidence of a lasting shift in foreign investor sentiment.What Should Stock Market Investors Do Now?Global money flows can change quickly. A market that faces sustained selling pressure today could become attractive tomorrow because of changing international investment preferences.However, investors should avoid making investment decisions solely on the basis of FPI buying or selling. Dalal recommends focusing on companies with strong fundamentals and reasonable valuations, particularly large-cap stocks.Companies with sound balance sheets, sustainable earnings and reasonable valuations could offer better resilience if global market conditions turn volatile again.{Disclaimer: Views expressed are those of the author in his capacity as Head of Broking & Research at Sanctum Wealth Private Limited, a SEBI-registered Research Analyst (Reg. No. INH000003051). The author and Sanctum Wealth may have financial interests in the securities discussed. Read the disclosures on www.sanctumwealth.com. Investments in securities markets are subject to market risks.}
news.summary: Share Market News: Despite recent inflows, investors should avoid interpreting the reversal as the beginning of a sustained foreign investment cycle.
